On Python 3.11, PySpark's pickler raises one from about 200 levels, under Python's default recursion limit, so a Column of about 200 to 745 levels pickles in the drop-in only. copy.copy and copy.deepcopy of a Column share its expression, of which a deep copy makes again only the levels above the UDFs whose functions it copies, so they copy a Column of any depth, as PySpark's copy.copy does; PySpark's copy.deepcopy raises a RecursionError from about 165 levels.

The frame bounds of Window.rowsBetween and rangeBetween are converted when the plan is built, as in PySpark: a bound of a row frame beyond an int, such as a start of -2**40 or of Window.unboundedFollowing, makes a window that shows it as it is, of which each request of a plan raises VALUE_NOT_BETWEEN, of the start and then of the end. A bound of True, which protobuf's int field refuses, or of an int beyond a long, which the window of the drop-in does not hold, raises at the call the error that PySpark raises when it builds the plan, the first of the start and of the end. The type of cast and try_cast is converted when the plan is built, as in PySpark: a StructField, the base DataType(), an abstract type such as AtomicType() and a Python subclass of them, also one nested in the type, make a Column that renders as the simpleString of the type, and whose plans raise PySpark's UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION.

Column.alias and Column.name raise PySpark's errors when PySpark's ColumnAlias raises them. At the call, they raise the metadata of several names (ONLY_ALLOWED_FOR_SINGLE_COLUMN) and other keywords. When a request builds the plan, they raise: - a name that protobuf refuses (a TypeError, or the UnicodeEncodeError or UnicodeDecodeError of UTF-8); - metadata of one name that json.dumps refuses; - metadata of no names (CANNOT_PROVIDE_METADATA).

So a Column that is not used raises none of these. The __repr__ of an alias of a name that is not a str (bytes too) raises the TypeError of PySpark's join of the names. A Column of such an alias copies and pickles, and its copy raises the same errors, also on a Python worker of the server. A str of lone surrogates, of a name or of another value of a Column (see below), shows escaped in the __repr__ of the Column (a\ud800b), where PySpark's shows it as it is: in upper case (\UD800) in the type of a cast, which the __repr__ upper-cases, and escaped twice in a list literal of Column.otherwise or getItem, which shows the repr of its strs.

The literal of a bytearray is of the bytes that it holds when the Column is made, which its __repr__ shows as PySpark's (Column<'bytearray(b'xy')'>), so a change to the bytearray after lit is in neither the __repr__ nor the plan, where PySpark's literal keeps the bytearray and shows and sends what it holds at the time. The literals of the core are immutable bytes, so its plans, pickles and copies never share a mutable Python object.

An Observation or a SparkSession.Hook, of the class or of a subclass (which a module defines in both clients), that PySpark pickled at protocol 0 or 1 raises a TypeError when the drop-in unpickles it, as CPython's copyreg._reconstructor cannot create the drop-in's, a class with a native base; protocols 2 and up, pickle's default, load in both clients, of the class or the subclass, and PySpark loads the drop-in's at every protocol. A hook of a subclass with __slots__ pickles at protocols 0 and 1 too, where PySpark's raises the TypeError of a class that defines __slots__ without __getstate__. A StorageLevel pickles at every protocol, and PySpark loads the drop-in's; one that PySpark pickled at 0 or 1 raises TypeError: object.__new__(StorageLevel) is not safe, use StorageLevel.__new__() when the drop-in unpickles it, and at the protocols 2 and up both clients load each other's.

So it is for the data types. PySpark's are plain classes, which pickle as their class and their __dict__: at the protocols 2 and up the drop-in makes its type of the class, without arguments, and sets the attributes, so a pickled df.schema loads with its fields, names, metadata, collations, nullable flags and parameters, as PySpark's types of them. The private _crs and _alg of PySpark's spatial types, which its constructors set of the SRID, are not attributes of the drop-in's. At protocol 0 or 1 the drop-in raises TypeError: object.__new__(DecimalType) is not safe, use DecimalType.__new__(). The drop-in's own types pickle, copy and deep-copy as _parse_datatype_json_string of their JSON, or, with a user-defined type, a nullable flag that is not a bool or a field of metadata, of the types and flags they are made of, which the Python workers of the server load at every protocol. So the copies of a struct, and of an array or a map of one, keep the metadata dicts of its fields as they are, which JSON does not (a tuple, a key that is not a str, the order of the keys), and are equal to it, as PySpark's pickle of the __dict__ is, and toNullable() makes each field of the dict of the field, as PySpark's metadata=field.metadata. A type of a state that its JSON does not keep, of an attribute that a user set, a hasPrecisionInfo that is not true, or the names and _needConversion of a StructType that an edit of its fields made differ, pickles and copies as its class and PySpark's __dict__ of it, as a type of a Python subclass does (see below), also in the types that hold it: the pickle of a type of no types in it, such as a DecimalType of an attribute, is PySpark's own, byte for byte. A shallow copy of a struct that pickles of its JSON is of new fields, where PySpark's shares the list of its fields. The class's own types compare without the attributes that a user set, where PySpark's comparison of the __dict__s holds them: a DecimalType(7, 3) of an attribute equals DecimalType(7, 3), where a type of a Python subclass compares them (see below).

A StructType caches its names as it is made and as add adds a field, as PySpark's, so an in-place change of its fields list, such as a StructField appended, leaves names and fieldNames() as they were. createDataFrame takes local rows, and the struct values below the top level, apart by those names, as PySpark's conversion reads fieldNames(), and converts their values by position with the fields as they are: a row of another number of values than the names raises AXIS_LENGTH_MISMATCH, a dict is read by them, and a field past them has no value (IndexError); below the top level, a value past the fields and fewer names than fields raise IndexError too. A pandas DataFrame is named with toDF(*schema.fieldNames()), of which the server raises for another number of names than columns. An element that is not a StructField is not taken (see dev/parity/known-differences.md).

The parameters of a type are its attributes, as PySpark's: t.scale = 3 makes a DecimalType(10, 2) a DecimalType(10, 3), as its repr, JSON, == and hash show, also in the struct, array or map that holds it. A drop-in type holds only the values that its constructor makes, so the assignment of another raises the constructor's error, where PySpark keeps it, of which its repr or JSON may fail later, as a field that an interval does not have (DayTimeIntervalType().startField = 9). So do the constructors: they refuse values that PySpark's keep, with a TypeError, such as DecimalType(10.0), TimeType(6.0), StringType(None) and the metadata [1] of a StructField, and hold the ints of those they take, so the precision of DecimalType(np.int64(12)) is an int, where PySpark's is the NumPy int. The assertions of PySpark's constructors (field name 1 should be a string, elementType string should be an instance of ...) are made under python -O too, which skips PySpark's, whose types are then made. The parameters that are types, the elementType of an ArrayType, the keyType and the valueType of a MapType and the dataType of a StructField, take a DataType or a DDL string, which they parse, where the constructors take a DataType only, as PySpark's assert it: ArrayType(LongType()).elementType = "string" makes it an ArrayType(StringType(), True), a DDL string that does not parse raises a ValueError and another value, None included, a TypeError, where PySpark keeps the value as it is given, which its repr shows (ArrayType(string, True)) and its json() fails of. A set srid of a spatial type is of its JSON too, where PySpark's JSON stays that of the CRS of its constructor. The parameters are not entries of the __dict__ of a type, so vars(t) is empty, where PySpark's has them. The type objects that an ArrayType, a MapType, a StructField and a StructType are given, by their constructors, add and the setters, are kept as they are, as PySpark's keep them, so a UserDefinedType whose module() or sqlType() is not implemented, such as UserDefinedType() itself, makes them: their repr, simpleString, needConversion, ==, hash, copies, pickles, tree string, names, add and toNullable are PySpark's, of the objects. A use that reads the JSON of the type raises the NOT_IMPLEMENTED of its jsonValue() then, as PySpark's does: json(), the plans of a cast, DataFrame.to, from_json, a table, a Java UDF and a UDTF, a reader's schema and the relation of data of no rows. toInternal and fromInternal raise the errors of the type's own methods. A cast to one is made and shows its simpleString(), as PySpark's Column, and raises its error at each request. createDataFrame of local rows or of a pandas DataFrame of one, also of local rows of values of such a type (its __UDT__), whose schema it infers first, of the errors of PySpark's inference, such as the CANNOT_MERGE_TYPE of the type and the type of a value of another row and the CANNOT_INFER_TYPE_FOR_FIELD of a value of no type, then converts the data, as PySpark's converters do, of the errors of the sqlType() and the serialize of the type, and then raises the error of its jsonValue(), of the json() of the schema.

The abstract classes of the types, DataType, AtomicType, NumericType, IntegralType, FractionalType, DatetimeType, AnyTimeType, SpatialType and AnsiIntervalType, make types of their own, as PySpark's plain classes do. AtomicType() has the typeName, simpleString and jsonValue of its class, atomic, converts no values, and is equal to a type of its class and __dict__ only. It pickles as its class and its __dict__: at the protocols 2 and up its pickle is PySpark's own, byte for byte, and PySpark loads the drop-in's at every protocol. The struct, array or map that holds it names it in its simpleString, JSON and tree string, and pickles of the types it is made of. It compares it, and names it in its simpleString and tree string, by the object that it holds, as PySpark's does, rather than by its JSON: so two types of the same JSON, of one class and different __dict__s or of two classes of one typeName, stay apart in the types that hold them, as UserDefinedTypes of other parameters do, and toNullable() keeps them as they are. The schema of a DataFrame and of its rows, as the server gives it, holds a new object of each user-defined type, as PySpark's UserDefinedType.fromJson makes it of its class, and so does fromJson: not the object that the client was given, nor of its attributes, and a class whose __init__ takes arguments raises its TypeError wherever PySpark converts that schema, as in PySpark: the schema, columns, dtypes, printSchema, the rows, the lookups that read the columns (df[0], dir(df), names of two underscores), the copies and the unpickles, the map functions and the numeric aggregations of grouped data. The cached schema of a DataFrame holds the objects that PySpark's _cached_schema holds, those of to or of a map function, else the new objects of the schema of the server: a set operation compares them as PySpark's does, by the __dict__ of their user-defined types, and a pickle carries them, which the unpickled DataFrame keeps as its cached schema. DataType.simpleString(t), the method of the base class, is t.typeName(), as PySpark's, which the types of a string of their own, such as bigint or struct<a:bigint>, override. IntegralType() is one instance, as PySpark's DataTypeSingleton makes it, and so is each Python subclass of it, of an instance of its own, and a Python subclass of the other classes, such as a UserDefinedType of parameters, takes the arguments of its __init__.

Neither client has a proto or an Arrow type of such a type, also of one nested in another or in the sqlType() of a user-defined type. A plan of one raises the UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION of PySpark's pyspark_types_to_proto_types, as PySpark's plans do: a cast, DataFrame.to, a UDF that is not Arrow-optimized, a UDTF, and transformWithState and transformWithStateInPandas of an output type of one at their first request, and the registration of a UDTF or of a Java UDF, Catalog.createTable and the schema of a table or a materialized view of a pipeline at the call or the decorator. As the schema of createDataFrame, local rows of one raise UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE_FOR_ARROW_CONVERSION once their values are converted, as PySpark's to_arrow_schema raises it after its converters run, so that the errors of the values, and of the serialize of a user-defined type, come first; and a pandas DataFrame of one as its only type raises UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE_FOR_ARROW. Data of no rows and a NumPy array make a relation of the JSON of the schema, PySpark's json(), in which such a type is its own JSON, also nested; the server fails to parse it (PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR), and so does a pyarrow Table of one as its only type. A reader's csv, json or xml of a DataFrame reads a schema of JSON as PySpark's Parse plan does when it is built, with StructType.fromJson, so each request of the DataFrame raises the CANNOT_PARSE_DATATYPE of the name of a type of its class only, and the UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE of a StructField as a type. DataType() and a Python subclass of it that is not an AtomicType are not expected as a schema, as PySpark's isinstance reads them: their NOT_EXPECTED_TYPE names their class.

PySpark's singleton types, from NullType and IntegerType to CalendarIntervalType and IntegralType, are classes of the metaclass DataTypeSingleton, which type(IntegerType) shows. The drop-in's are native classes, whose metaclass is type: PyO3 has no option of a metaclass of a class, and CPython refuses to assign the __class__ of a class of type after it is made. So an error that names the type of such a class, as the NOT_EXPECTED_TYPE of udf(f, IntegerType) (of the class, not of an instance), names type where PySpark's names DataTypeSingleton. pyspark.sql.types has PySpark's DataTypeSingleton, of which a class is made as PySpark's makes it, such as a subclass of a singleton type of __main__, which PySpark's cloudpickle sends by value of its metaclass: it loads, of one instance, as in PySpark. The constructors of the native classes return the one instance and raise the TypeError of DataTypeSingleton.__call__ for an argument, as PySpark's, and inspect.signature of the class shows no parameters. A copy, a deep copy and a pickle of the one instance are the one instance too, where PySpark's copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle make another object of the class, as the note of its DataTypeSingleton says. A subclass of such a class of another metaclass, class X(IntegerType, metaclass=Meta), is made, where PySpark's raises the TypeError of a metaclass conflict.

PySpark's concrete types are plain classes too, which a user subclasses, and so are the drop-in's, from NullType and StringType to ArrayType, StructField and StructType. A type of a Python subclass is of the core type of its class, which the plans and the conversions read, as PySpark's read it by isinstance, and the methods of its class are PySpark's, of the methods of the object: - typeName() is the name of the subclass (subinteger of class SubIntegerType(IntegerType)), of which simpleString(), jsonValue() and json() are, where the class has none of its own, and the type of the JSON of an array, a map and a struct; the repr of a class whose repr names its class names the subclass (SubBooleanType(), SubDayTimeIntervalType(0, 3)), and so does its hash, of the repr; - where a method of PySpark's calls another method of the object, or of a type that an array, a map or a struct holds, the drop-in's calls it too, so an override of a subclass is of their JSON, simple string, repr, tree string and conversions, also on the Python workers of the server, to which a UDF pickles its return type: a UDF that is not Arrow-optimized converts its results with the toInternal of the subclass, as PySpark's; - the conversion of the local rows of createDataFrame takes the type objects of the schema, as PySpark's converters hold them: its errors name the object (input for SubBooleanType() must not be None), of its repr, and a geometry or a geography converts with the toInternal of a subclass, whose result is converted as PyArrow converts it; - a type of a subclass is equal only to a type of its class or of a subclass of it, of the same parameters and of the same attributes of its __dict__, as PySpark's isinstance(other, self.__class__) and __dict__: StringType() == SubStringType() is false in both orders, as == calls the __eq__ of the subclass first; - its __init__ takes arguments of its own, which the __new__ of the class takes as object.__new__ does, and passes the parameters to the __init__ of the class, which sets them, as PySpark's, also of StringType, DecimalType, TimeType, the intervals and StructType, whose errors of arguments are those of __init__ (DecimalType.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'foo'), but for the counts of too many positional arguments, which are PyO3's, without self, as for the other methods (see below): DecimalType.__init__() takes from 0 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given, where PySpark's says "from 1 to 3" and "4"; - it pickles, copies and deep-copies, at the protocols 2 and up, as copyreg.__newobj__(cls) and PySpark's __dict__ of it, of its parameters (and of the _crs and _alg of a spatial type) and of the attributes that a user set, and of its __slots__, so each client loads the other's, and cloudpickle sends a class of __main__ by value: the pickle of a type of no types in it, such as a DecimalType of a subclass, is PySpark's own, byte for byte, and the types that a type holds pickle as the class's own do (see above); - a subclass of a singleton type has an instance of its own, as PySpark's DataTypeSingleton makes it, and takes no arguments; - the Column of a cast or try_cast to it renders its simpleString(), as PySpark's (CAST(id AS SUB)), and so does one to a user-defined type of its own simpleString() (CAST(id AS SCALE2)), also in an array, a map or a struct, while the plan is of the core type.

What differs: - The parameters are not entries of the __dict__ of the type, as for the class's own types (vars(t) holds the attributes that a user set), and a subclass whose __init__ does not call the __init__ of its class has the parameters of cls.__new__(cls), of the defaults of the class (StringType(), DecimalType(10, 0), an array of NullType()), where PySpark's has none of them and raises the AttributeError of each that a method reads. - Python calls the __init__ of a subclass of a singleton type at each call of the class, which returns the one instance, where PySpark's metaclass calls it on the first call, as the drop-in's DataTypeSingleton does of a class of it, such as of PySpark's cloudpickle of such a subclass of __main__ (see above). Copies and pickles of the instance are the instance, as for the class's own. - A subclass of __slots__ pickles at the protocols 0 and 1 too, as copyreg.__newobj__(cls) of its state, where PySpark's raises TypeError: a class that defines __slots__ without defining __getstate__ cannot be pickled. - The repr of an array, a map, a field or a struct that holds a type whose repr has a str that UTF-8 cannot encode, such as one of a lone surrogate, raises its UnicodeEncodeError, and so do their str() and hash, of the repr, where PySpark's make them. DataFrame.to of such a struct of a type that has no proto, of a subclass of DataType, raises it at the call, where PySpark's raises the UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION of the type at the first request. - A class of type classes of two branches of their hierarchy, such as class X(StringType, IntegerType), raises TypeError: multiple bases have instance lay-out conflict, as CPython raises of bases of conflicting layouts, where PySpark makes the class. - createDataFrame of data sends the JSON of the core types of its schema, where PySpark sends the json() of the schema object, which names a type of a subclass by its typeName() ("subinteger") and which the server then fails to parse (PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR), so sending it would only bring back that failure; of data of no rows it sends the json() of the object, as PySpark. The readers, from_json, from_xml, applyInPandasWithState and toDDL send the json() of the object, as PySpark's.

The metadata of a field is the dict that it was given, which == compares as Python compares dicts, as PySpark compares the __dict__s of its fields, also in a struct and in the types that hold it: (1, 2) is not [1, 2], nor {1: "a"} {"1": "a"}, nor 10**30 10**30 + 1. Its jsonValue() holds that dict, which json() writes with json.dumps, as PySpark's: an int of more than 64 bits as it is, a float as Python's repr writes it, of the shortest digits that read back as it and of an even last digit of a tie (1e-07, and 74334700308107.62 of 74334700308107.625), NaN and Infinity, and the keys sorted as sort_keys sorts them, of the ints and floats by their values ({10: "a", 9: "b"} is {"9":"b","10":"a"}). The core holds the metadata of the JSON of json.dumps of the dict, of its values as they are written, so a plan sends that text, as PySpark's pyspark_types_to_proto_types sends the metadata of a field, and so do the readers and createDataFrame in the JSON of the schema that they send, of any depth, also of the metadata of the fields of the sqlType() of a UserDefinedType, as PySpark's: of a schema that was given, or of one inferred of local rows, of the __UDT__ objects of their values, of their own jsonValue(). The server keeps the low 64 bits of such an int (10**30 becomes 5076944270305263616), and refuses a float that is not finite. The Arrow schema of createDataFrame of a pyarrow Table holds json.dumps of the metadata of each field, as PySpark's to_arrow_schema writes it; that of local rows, of a pandas DataFrame, of each of its conversions of a column, and of a numpy array holds it on the fields of the sqlType() of a UserDefinedType only, as PySpark's _deduplicate_field_names drops the metadata of the others, which names the fields of each struct of the schema (a_0, a_1), of the top level too for a pandas DataFrame, but not those of the sqlType(). A dict that json.dumps refuses, such as one of a set or of a key of a tuple, is kept, and only the uses that write its JSON raise the error of json.dumps, as PySpark's: json(), of its sorted keys too ('<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'), each request of a plan of the type, such as of a cast, also of one made in the sqlType() that jsonValue() calls, and createDataFrame, after it converts the data, of the error of its Arrow schema first where that holds the metadata (keys must be str, int, float, bool or None, not tuple). mapInPandas, mapInArrow, applyInPandas and applyInArrow, after they read the columns of the DataFrame, and those of a cogroup raise PySpark's NOT_IMPLEMENTED of the return type of such a schema, of their UDF's check of its Arrow type. The JSON of a type writes each character of its names and strings that is not printable ASCII as the \u escape of json.dumps, as PySpark's json().

A TableArg, of DataFrame.asTable(), pickles at every protocol, plainly and by cloudpickle, as PySpark's, of its user-set attributes, and copy.copy and copy.deepcopy copy it as PySpark's. Its pickle keeps the relation of the plan of its DataFrame, as a pickled DataFrame does (see "What a plan build does for a pickle" in dev/parity/known-differences.md), of the functions of its UDFs, and its partitioning, ordering and single partition; the unpickle sends no request, as PySpark's, and the table argument that it gives sends the same plan and subquery, of the same plan ID, whose functions its requests pickle. A plain pickle of one of a function that does not pickle by reference, such as a lambda, fails at it, as PySpark's. A plan that does not build pickles too, and the requests of the unpickled table argument raise its error, as PySpark's. The pickle names the session of its DataFrame by its ID, so it unpickles only where the session of that ID is active, as a pickled DataFrame does: it raises NO_ACTIVE_SESSION where none is, such as on another thread, and PySparkAssertionError where another one is, where PySpark's, whose plan holds no session, unpickles anywhere. On a Python worker of the server it unpickles as PySpark Connect's table argument of the relation, which needs no session. Its _subquery_expr is an expression of pyspark.sql.connect.expressions, as a Column's _expr is, of PySpark's to_plan and repr, which is made at each access as a property of the native class: vars() of the table argument does not show it and it cannot be set, where PySpark's is an instance attribute, a SubqueryExpression with the fields of the subquery. _is_partitioned() is PySpark's.

The __repr__ of a Column of a subquery names its plan by its plan ID, SubqueryExpression(plan=<plan 2>, type=scalar), where PySpark's shows the repr of its plan object, <pyspark.sql.connect.plan.Project object at 0x...>.

DataFrame.inputFiles() returns a list of its paths, where PySpark returns protobuf's repeated field of the response, a RepeatedScalarContainer, which compares equal to the list.

The keys of getMessageParameters() of a server error are in the server's order. PySpark's follow the protobuf map of the error details that it fetches: with protobuf's pure-Python implementation that is the server's order too, and with upb, protobuf's default, the order of its hash table, which changes from one process to the next. For its own errors, PySpark keeps the order of each call site.

A signal ends the wait of a call for the server as it ends PySpark's. The KeyboardInterrupt of a handler, as of Ctrl-C, interrupts the execution in flight on the server, as the except KeyboardInterrupt of PySpark's execution does, and a second signal ends the wait without waiting for the interrupt; the exception of another handler ends the wait at once and is raised, without an interrupt. The lookup of the plan compression settings of the first plan of a session, and the read of the stack-trace settings of an error, catch the exception of a handler that is an Exception, as the except Exception of PySpark's do: the lookup is then of no settings, as a failed one, and the call goes on and waits again.

At interpreter exit, a session that is not stopped has its ML cache cleaned by one clean_cache request, as PySpark's client does. Its errors are ignored, but when the server is gone the exit waits on that request's retries, as PySpark's does, so the exit can take as long as those retries. A signal ends that wait, as it ends PySpark's, whose cleanup catches Exception only: the KeyboardInterrupt of Ctrl-C is raised out of the exit hook, which atexit reports before it runs the next one, and the session is then neither released nor closed. The exception of a handler that is an Exception ends the request that waits, which the exit hook goes on from, unless it arrives while the session looks the plan compression settings up for the clean_cache, as for its first plan: the lookup catches it, as PySpark's, and the clean_cache is sent, which waits again. A stopped session sends nothing at exit. PySpark 4.3.0 does not exit at all while a session other than its default one is left open to the end, such as one of newSession() or of SparkSession(connection=...): its SparkSession.__del__ closes the client in the teardown of the interpreter, whose grpcio Channel.close() waits forever, a bug of PySpark that the drop-in does not reproduce: it exits. Nor does a session that the program dropped send anything, of which no object is left but a conf or a client of it: neither the session nor a DataFrame, reader, writer, catalog, stream or ML object of it. PySpark's session object closes its client when it is freed, and the exit sends nothing for a closed client. The drop-in drops such a session, closes its client, and closes the connection of the process to its server once no session uses it, which the sessions of newSession() and cloneSession() share, as PySpark's channels share their subchannels, but a session of a token, whose connection is its own. Once its catalog or streams is read, PySpark's session object is in a reference cycle, which only the garbage collector frees, so that until a collection its exit still cleans its ML cache; the drop-in's session has no such cycle and is freed at once, as PySpark's is by a collection. A client that no session object owns, of SparkConnectClient(...) or of its newSession() or clone(), lives until the exit, as PySpark's atexit registration keeps it, so its ML cache is cleaned at exit unless it is closed, even when the program dropped it. SPARK_CONNECT_RELEASE_SESSION_ON_EXIT is read when a session is made, as PySpark reads it: when it is true or 1, the session is then also released and closed at exit, after the cleanup.

PySpark's client sends the ReleaseExecute requests of an execution through a ThreadPoolExecutor, which refuses new work once the interpreter has begun to shut down. The drop-in refuses them from the same point. An execution after it, such as a collect() in an atexit handler, raises RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown after its first response and sends no ReleaseExecute, as in PySpark. The exit's clean_cache ends the same way, and its error is ignored. Requests that are not executions, such as the AnalyzePlan of a schema, still work then.

The TypeError for too many positional arguments counts them without self: where CPython says "takes from 2 to 4 positional arguments but 5 were given", the drop-in says "takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given". A method that takes no arguments gets "takes no arguments (1 given)", where CPython says "takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given" for DataFrame.distinct(1). A method that takes one argument gets the plural "positional arguments" even for a count of one: the drop-in says "takes 1 positional arguments but 3 were given" for DataFrame.limit(1, 2, 3), where CPython says "takes 2 positional arguments but 4 were given". These are the messages of PyO3 0.29.3, whose too_many_positional_arguments (src/impl_/extract_argument.rs) counts the parameters of the Rust function, of no self, and writes "positional arguments" of any count: matching CPython's would need a patched PyO3.

A warning that the extension raises, such as the FutureWarning of registerTempTable, Catalog.registerFunction, createExternalTable, a dbName of the catalog, and getItem and getField of a Column, and the UserWarning of replace of a dict and a value, of GroupedData.apply, of type hints that applyInPandas and applyInArrow cannot read, of the arguments that createDataFrame ignores, of the configurations of the server, and of the listener bus of the streams, is attributed as PySpark's is: to the module of pyspark.sql.connect of PySpark's warnings.warn, of the registry of the warnings that the module showed, and to the line of that call, in the file of the drop-in's module of that name. So warnings.filterwarnings(..., module="pyspark") and the filters of a line match it, and the default filter shows it once, as PySpark's. The drop-in's module ends before that line, so the warning shows no source line, where PySpark's shows its call. The warning of a window of no partitions, WARN WindowExpression: No Partition Defined for Window operation! ..., is PySpark's: a UserWarning of pyspark.sql.connect.expressions, of its line 1126, which the default filter shows once, at each request that builds the plan of such a window, as PySpark warns as it builds the plan. A pickle of a DataFrame or a Column does not warn, as PySpark's builds no plan; but PySpark's unpickle of a DataFrame warns once, as it builds the plan to read the columns of the new DataFrame, where the drop-in's does not; and a DataFrame, a Column or a table argument that is unpickled sends the plan that was built for the pickle, of the functions of its UDFs pickled at each request (see the UDFs below), so its requests do not warn again, where PySpark's warn at each. Such a plan keeps the origin of the and of the conditions of a join of a list of Columns of that time too, where PySpark gives it the call site of each request that builds it, as it does in the drop-in otherwise. A copy of a DataFrame, in its session or another, builds its plan at each request, and warns then, as PySpark's. A request that PySpark builds in functools, as of isStreaming, a functools.cached_property, gives that and the call site of functools.py, where the drop-in gives the user's.

The FutureWarning of BisectingKMeansModel.computeCost is attributed as PySpark's is, to the line of its warnings.warn in pyspark/ml/clustering.py and to the module pyspark.ml.clustering, of its registry of shown warnings, so the filters of that module match it.

The TypeError for a bad keyword argument of a method that takes no **options is PyO3's, which CPython words differently in two cases. For a key that is not a str, as df.limit(1, **{1: 2}), CPython says "keywords must be strings", where the drop-in says "DataFrame.limit() got an unexpected keyword argument '1'". For a method that takes no arguments, as df.count(foo=1), CPython says "DataFrame.count() got an unexpected keyword argument 'foo'", where the drop-in says "DataFrame.count() takes no keyword arguments". The methods that take **options, and the readers', writers' and SparkSession.builder.config's that take named options, word both as CPython does.

A str that UTF-8 cannot encode, such as one with a lone surrogate, fails where PySpark builds the request that carries it, which is not always the call that takes it. The error is PySpark's UnicodeEncodeError with the same message, and no request is sent: - a reader's format, schema, option key or value, path or table name fails the DataFrame when its plan is built, at its first request, such as df.schema; - a DataFrameWriter's or a DataFrameWriterV2's format or provider, option, table property, partitioning, bucketing, sorting or clustering column, path or table name fails the write, such as save, saveAsTable or create; - a withColumns name, or an as-of join's how or direction, fails the DataFrame when its plan is built, at its first request, such as collect or columns. A direction of bytes that are not UTF-8 fails there with PySpark's UnicodeDecodeError, as protobuf's string field gives it; - the names of createDataFrame of a pandas DataFrame, of its column labels or of a list, and of a pyarrow Table, which PySpark applies with toDF, fail the DataFrame when its plan is built, at its first request. Those of other data, local rows or a NumPy array, which PySpark's conversion names its table by, fail the call, as PySpark's, which reads the settings of its conversions first, where the drop-in sends no request; - the names, SQL strings and literal strs of Columns fail each DataFrame whose plan has the Column when its plan is built, while the Column is made, renders, copies and pickles: those of F.col, F.expr, F.lit and the other functions, df[name], df.name, colRegex, metadataColumn, the field of getField, withField and dropFields, the function of call_function and call_udf, the type of cast and try_cast, and the column names and keywords of a UDF or UDTF call; - so do the arguments of the methods of a DataFrame, of its na and stat, and of grouped data that their plans set as they are given, such as the alias of alias, the names of withColumn(s)Renamed, withMetadata, toDF, drop, dropDuplicates, withWatermark, unpivot, describe, summary, crosstab, freqItems and the NA functions, a hint, the name of observe, the names of a using join, the name of zipWithIndex, the functions of agg of a dict, the output mode and the timeout of applyInPandasWithState, and the output mode, the time mode and the event-time column of transformWithStateInPandas and transformWithState, and the name of an Observation, which fails the DataFrames that it observes; - the schema of from_avro and to_avro, and the message name and the descriptor set of from_protobuf and to_protobuf, are literals, as PySpark's lit of them, which PySpark does not check otherwise: such a str fails each DataFrame of the Column, and a message name of another type, such as 5, bytes or None, is the server's error of the function; - a tag of addTag fails each execution that the thread starts, as its request is built after its plan, until removeTag removes it; a request without tags, such as that of df.schema, is sent. getTags gives the tag as it is; - a key or a value of SparkSession.builder.config, or an appName, fails getOrCreate; - a DataStreamWriter's fails the call that takes it, as PySpark sets that writer's request as it goes.

Such a str is not one of the modes of explain, of the how of dropna, of the join types of join and lateralJoin, of the modes, directions and join types of nearestByJoin, nor a column of sum, avg, min and max of grouped data: they raise PySpark's VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED, UNSUPPORTED_JOIN_TYPE, the NEAREST_BY_JOIN errors and NOT_NUMERIC_COLUMNS, of the str as it is. So is the UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION of to and of a cast of such a str, or of another object whose str has a lone surrogate. nearestByJoin reads the lower() of its mode, direction and join type, as PySpark's, so an object without one raises its AttributeError, bytes as a join type the TypeError of replace, and bytes as a mode or a direction its error, of the bytes as they are. Such a str is no name of readStream.name, which raises INVALID_STREAMING_SOURCE_NAME of it, as PySpark's re.match(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$", name) does not match it; that pattern matches a name of a final newline, which the server refuses. A Column's attribute of such a name is the field of that name, as col[name], so hasattr of it is True, and a session's raises the AttributeError of object.__getattribute__, so hasattr of it is False, as in PySpark. explain builds the plan first, so the error of a plan that fails to build comes first.

The commands that PySpark sends when they are called set their names as protobuf converts them, at the call: registerJavaFunction and registerJavaUDAF (the name, then the class), the register of spark.udf of a UDF and of spark.udtf, the name() of the class of spark.dataSource.register, interruptTag and interruptOperation take bytes of UTF-8, and raise protobuf's TypeError "bad argument type for built-in operation" of another value; interruptTag(None) and interruptOperation(None) raise the AssertionError of PySpark's request. The register of a plain function names the function of its UDF first, so a name that is not a str raises the TypeError of __name__, as PySpark's. A function registered of the name None is registered as fun_ and a random hex, as PySpark's client does, and register returns its UDF. SparkSession.builder.master of Spark Connect takes any value and does nothing, as PySpark Connect's.

So it is for the other values that a plan sets as they are given, which protobuf converts when it builds the plan: a string field takes bytes of UTF-8, such as alias(b"q"), and refuses another object with the TypeError "bad argument type for built-in operation", such as the alias 5 or None, the names of withColumnRenamed(1, "z"), unpivot, describe(b"ab") (of its ints), freqItems(["a", 1]), the subset of na.replace, and a using join on ["a", 1]; an int field refuses an int beyond it with a ValueError, such as fillna(2**70), dropna(thresh=2**40) and the arguments of spark.range and spark.tvf.range after their int(), and a bool with a TypeError, such as dropna(thresh=True); a double field refuses a str, such as the support of freqItems. A join on a tuple, or on a list of conditions whose & fails, such as of a Column and an object that is neither a Column nor a literal, raises the AttributeError of to_plan or of &, which PySpark computes when it builds the plan, such as the PySparkAttributeError of the _expr of a Row; an exception of & of another class, such as a KeyError of an object's __getattr__, is raised by the join. Of several such values, the requests raise the error of the first in the order in which PySpark builds the plan: the input of a plan before the plan, but for the partitioning of a repartition, which comes first, and its count of partitions, which comes after its input, and the name of a hint or an observation before its expressions; the order of the other values of one plan can differ. As in PySpark, a DataFrame of such a plan raises at its requests, schema and collect() among them, and the call raises none. Of a join on a tuple, or on a list of conditions whose & fails, the properties read the Column of _schema, as PySpark's: their self._schema raises an AttributeError, after which Python calls the __getattr__ of the DataFrame, of that name. So schema gives a deep copy of the Column, columns, dtypes, the representation, dir(), the key completions and toArrow raise the NOT_ITERABLE of iterating it, and printSchema the TypeError of a call of a Column. The drop-in's DataFrame has no _schema itself, so df._schema is the Column of that name, where PySpark's is the schema.

A DataFrame whose plan fails to build pickles, also by cloudpickle, and its unpickle raises the error, as PySpark's: its pickle keeps the objects of the plan, and its unpickle builds the plan to read the columns of the new DataFrame. Of an AttributeError, such as of a join on a tuple or on a list of conditions whose & fails, PySpark's read of the columns falls back from its _schema to the Column of __getattr__, whose fields is a Column, which is not iterable: so the unpickle, a copy.copy and a copy.deepcopy, which read the columns too, raise NOT_ITERABLE, in both. alias, a hint, dropDuplicates, observe, filter, sort, sortWithinPartitions and the repartitions of such a value keep the cached schema of the DataFrame that they are of, as PySpark copies it, so their schema is known without a request, and their other requests raise the error.

The barrier of mapInPandas and mapInArrow is a protobuf bool, which their plan sets once it pickled the function, when it is built: an int is taken, as barrier=1, and another value, such as "x", None or a float, fails each request with the TypeError of protobuf, and not the call. The DataFrame keeps its schema, of the schema that it is given, as PySpark's _map_partitions caches it: a StructType as the object that it is, so schema gives a copy of it as it is then, and columns and dtypes its fields then, as do those of applyInPandas, applyInArrow and the cogroup's; the type of a DDL string is parsed at the call. The plan reads profile.id of its resource profile after that, so the profile is created on the server by the first request that builds the plan, such as collect, and not by the call nor by schema, as in PySpark; a profile without an id, such as a str, fails the requests with that AttributeError, and the id of a request whose flag fails is not read.

A merge builder keeps its condition and the conditions of its clauses as they are given, as PySpark's: mergeInto(table, 5) and whenMatched(5) raise nothing, the clause's action raises the AttributeError of the to_plan that 5 lacks, and so does the merge of a condition of mergeInto. An action builds its assignments as PySpark's _build_merge_action, in the order of assignments.items(), in which the merge sends them, and raises their errors in that order, before those of the condition: a key that is not a str, bytes too, is the bare AssertionError of PySpark's expr, a value that is not a Column the AttributeError of its to_plan, and an object that is not a mapping the AttributeError of its items.

A str that a later call unsets or replaces is no longer in the request, in the same cases as in PySpark. A stream reader's option of None leaves its option as it was, as PySpark's does. A batch reader's removes the option, which PySpark's plans of table and changes set, failing their requests (see dev/parity/known-differences.md). An option key, a table property or a config key that is not a str fails at the same call as PySpark's, with the same error: an AssertionError at a reader's load of a path, and protobuf's TypeError where the request is built otherwise.

The function of a UDF, of a pandas or Arrow UDF of any eval type, of a UDTF (called, of a table argument, in a lateral join) and of mapInPandas, mapInArrow, applyInPandas, applyInArrow, the cogroup's applyInPandas and applyInArrow, applyInPandasWithState, transformWithStateInPandas and transformWithState is pickled each time a request builds a plan that holds it, as PySpark's PythonUDF.to_plan and PythonUDTF.to_plan pickle it. So a value that the function reads, changed after the function was applied and before an action, is the value that the action runs with, and so for each later action. The output type of a UDF and of a map or group-map function is converted then too, of the type object that PySpark's PythonUDF keeps, as are the return type of a UDTF, of the object that its PythonUDTF keeps, the output schema of transformWithState and transformWithStateInPandas and the schema of DataFrame.to: a StructType changed in place after the call, as by add or by a field renamed, is the type that the request sends, and that the pickled command of a UDF carries, as it is then. A type that the conversion does not take, such as AtomicType() or a StructField as a type, fails the requests with its UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION, not the call, where the eval type of the UDF does not refuse it at the call, as the Arrow and pandas ones do with NOT_IMPLEMENTED. A function that does not pickle fails each request of the plan, from the first, such as df.schema, with PySpark's error, the PicklingError of CloudPickleSerializer.dumps, or UDTF_SERIALIZATION_ERROR of a UDTF, and no request is sent; the call that applies it does not fail. The functions are pickled in the order in which PySpark builds the plan, the initial state of transformWithState before its function and the arguments of a UDTF before its handler, and the first error of the build, of a pickling or of a value that the plan does not take, such as a str above, is raised. The return type of a UDTF is converted after its arguments and before its handler is pickled, as PySpark's PythonUDTF.to_plan converts it with pyspark_types_to_proto_types, of the PythonUDTF that the call made: of the return type object and the handler class of the UDTF at the call, a str as its UnparsedDataType, and of the __name__ of the class then, which UDTF_SERIALIZATION_ERROR names; so a returnType or a func set on the UDTF after the call is not that of the call. A value that is neither a DataType nor a str, such as 5, is kept by the UDTF as it is, and each request of a call of it raises UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION of data type 5, of the str of the value when the request is built, or the error of that str; so does a type that has no proto, such as AtomicType(), also one that a type changed after the call holds. spark.udf.register and spark.udtf.register are commands, which pickle the function when they are called, as PySpark's do; spark.udtf.register and spark.client.register_udtf set the name and convert the return type first, as it is then, and the latter reads the __name__ of the handler class before them, as PySpark's PythonUDTF does. A copy of a Column, a DataFrame, grouped data or a table argument holds the functions, which the requests of the copy pickle, as PySpark's: copy.copy shares them, and copy.deepcopy deep-copies each with the memo of the call, so a function, a lambda or a closure is the function itself, and a callable object, a bound method or a functools.partial is a copy, which the copies of one call share, as the two Columns of a UDF of copy.deepcopy([c1, c2]) do. copy.copy shares the output type of a UDF and the return type of a UDTF too, and copy.deepcopy copies them, as PySpark's copy of the plan does: a type changed in place after a deep copy is not that of the copy, nor one changed after a pickle that of the unpickled DataFrame. A request warns once of a window of no partitions, as PySpark's, in the order of the build, though the drop-in builds the plan of a request twice when it has such functions, as it pickles them between the two builds: a window that comes after a function in the build warns in its turn among the picklings, so a function before it that does not pickle raises the error of its pickling without the warning, and the error of the warning, of an "error" filter of the warnings, is raised before the functions after the window are pickled, as PySpark's.

A pickled Column, DataFrame or table argument carries the functions of its UDFs, as PySpark's pickle carries those of its plan objects: the (func, returnType) of a UDF, the handler class, its name and the return type of a UDTF, and the schema of DataFrame.to, which the requests of the unpickled object convert and pickle when they build its plan, of the holes in place of their commands in the relation or the expression of the pickle, also on the server's Python worker, where PySpark's plan pickles them. So pickle.dumps of one of a UDF of a lambda raises the error of pickling the lambda, as PySpark's, and of a function that pickle pickles by reference, such as a function of a module or of __main__, pickles, of the function by its name, which the requests of the unpickled object pickle as it is then: a value that the function reads, changed after the pickle, is the value that they send, and a function that does not pickle then fails them with the PicklingError of CloudPickleSerializer.dumps. cloudpickle.dumps of a function that does not pickle by value raises the error of pickling it, such as the TypeError of a lock that it reads, as PySpark's, and CloudPickleSerializer.dumps its PicklingError. A plain pickle of a DataFrame fails at the first function that it does not pickle, and else at the function that gives back its session, as PySpark's pickles its plan and then its session. An output type of a UDF or a return type of a UDTF that the build of the plan does not convert, such as AtomicType() of a UDF without Arrow, or a StructType changed to hold it after the call, does not fail the pickle: as PySpark's, which keeps the type object, the requests of the unpickled Column and table argument raise its UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION, and so does the unpickle of a DataFrame, which builds its plan.

A pickled Column of subqueries, of scalar(), exists(), isin of a DataFrame or a table argument, carries the relations of the plans that they refer to, of their plan IDs, as PySpark's carries the plan objects of its subqueries, which keep their _plan_id: a plan of the unpickled Column sends them in its WithRelations, as a plan of the Column does, also on the server's Python worker, where the Column is PySpark Connect's. Column._expr pickles as the expression of the unpickled Column, and TableArg._subquery_expr as that of a Column of its subquery, as PySpark's expressions pickle their fields. A pickled, cloudpickled or deep-copied Column keeps the origins of its expressions, of their call sites, as PySpark's unpickled expressions keep their origin, whether the capture of origins is on or not (is_debugging_enabled): so does a sort order or a CASE WHEN, which the unpickle makes again of its parts, and the sort orders of a window specification or of a table argument.

A DataFrame or a Column reports the functions of its UDFs to Python's garbage collector, as PySpark's plan of Python objects is seen by it, so a reference cycle through a function and the DataFrame or the Column that holds it, such as through a bound method of an object that keeps the DataFrame, is collected. It also reports the plans of the Python client that it holds, as PySpark's DataFrame and Column hold their plan objects: the plan of a DataFrame(plan, session), which its relation keeps, also through the subqueries of the expressions of a plan, and the plan that an unpickled Column of the subquery of a DataFrame of a plan that did not build keeps, to build it at its requests. So a cycle through such a plan and a DataFrame of it, a DataFrame over a subquery of it, a Column of its subquery or a table argument of it, such as through an attribute of the plan that keeps the object, is collected. So do the objects that hold such Columns, or the plan of a DataFrame, as PySpark's do: grouped data and their cogroups, a table argument, a window specification, the writers of write, writeTo and writeStream, na and stat, a merge builder and its clauses, the generator of toLocalIterator, which holds its DataFrame until it ends, as PySpark's generator holds self, and the expression of a Column (Column._expr) and of a table argument (TableArg._subquery_expr), which copy.copy and copy.deepcopy copy as they copy a Column. Those that hold their DataFrame report it, and the DataFrame reports the functions of the plan that they share, so a cycle through the DataFrame alone, such as df.back = df.groupBy("id"), is collected too. So do the DataFrames of the plan of another, DataFrame(df._plan, session), copy.copy(df) and a copy.deepcopy(df) that copies no function or Observation of the plan, which keep df and report it, as PySpark's DataFrames of one plan object both hold the object: a cycle through the functions of the plan and either of them, or both, is collected. Such a DataFrame keeps the whole of df alive, its attributes, the schema that it cached and its executionInfo with its plan, where PySpark's keeps the plan object alone, until the DataFrame is freed. An ArrayType, a MapType, a StructField and a StructType report the type objects, the flags and the metadata dict that they hold, and the lists of a struct, as PySpark's __dict__ holds them, so a cycle through a type that one holds, such as a DecimalType with an attribute that keeps the struct, is collected. A function or a plan of the Python client that two of these objects share, through one Rust value of a plan or of an expression that both hold, is reported by neither: a Column and a DataFrame of it; a Column and its expression (Column._expr), its copy.copy or its copy.deepcopy, which share its expression, but for the UDFs that a deep copy copies and the nodes above them; two DataFrames of plans of their own, such as a DataFrame and one derived from it; and a DataFrame and a Column of its subquery, or a table argument of it, which holds its plan and not the DataFrame, as PySpark's does. They share one reference to it, which the collector would count as that of the one that reports it, so it could free the object with that one while the other lives and reaches it. A cycle that keeps both, such as through a plan of the Python client whose attribute keeps both its DataFrame and a Column of its subquery, is freed only when it is broken, where PySpark collects it. A stream writer holds its DataFrame, where PySpark's holds the plan, so a DataFrame that keeps its stream writer is freed by the collector, where PySpark frees it with its last reference. The functions of foreachBatch and foreach are kept as their pickles, as PySpark's stream writer keeps them, so a function that keeps its writer is freed with its last reference, and a copy or a pickle of the writer carries the pickle of the call. The registration of dataSource reports its session, and the builder of pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession its channel builder and the list of its hook factories, which its shallow copies share, as PySpark's plain objects hold them, so a session that keeps its dataSource, or a channel builder or a hook factory that keeps its builder or a copy of it, is collected. The readers, the writers and the builder report the keys and the values of their options that are objects, which PySpark's dicts of options keep as they are, such as a key that is not a str, and the format, the save mode, the partitioning and clustering columns and the provider that the writers keep as they are, through one object of them that their shallow copies share, as PySpark's copies share the dict of their options and the _write of a writer: so a cycle through one, such as a key of an option that keeps its reader, is collected, also with a copy of the reader, and freed with the last of the copies.

The condition and the assignments of a clause of mergeInto are built, and the functions of their UDFs pickled, when the clause is added, which raises there, and the merge sends them as they were built then, as PySpark's sends the protos that _build_merge_action built for the clause: so a value that a function reads, changed after the clause, is not that of the merge, also of a copy of the builder, and a window of no partitions of a clause warns once, at the clause.

A UDF and a UDTF are of PySpark Connect's classes, UserDefinedFunction of pyspark.sql.connect.udf and UserDefinedTableFunction of pyspark.sql.connect.udtf, as in PySpark. The classic pyspark.sql.udf and pyspark.sql.udtf are PySpark's modules, of Apache Spark as they are, whose classes, which pyspark.sql.functions names too, need a SparkContext: so isinstance of a UDTF that udtf builds against the classic UserDefinedTableFunction is False, as in PySpark. udf gives a function in both clients, which is of neither class.

So it is for the objects of a session: each is of PySpark Connect's class, of its module of pyspark.sql.connect, as repr, type(x).__module__ and pickle show it. These are the SparkSession, its conf, catalog, read, readStream, streams, udf, udtf, dataSource, tvf and client, and a DataFrame's write, writeTo, writeStream, mergeInto and its clauses, na, stat, groupBy, cogroup, asTable and the WindowSpec of its windows, and an Observation. So are SparkSession.Hook, nested in the session class, and the classes of the client, which pyspark.sql.connect.client.core defines, as PySpark's: its channel builders, SparkConnectClient and RpcDeadlines, of its __all__, which its package names too, and PlanObservedMetrics, AnalyzeResult and ConfigResult, which only core names. The functions of these classes are of core too, where inspect finds their source, and their pickles and those of the results are PySpark's. The package pyspark.sql.connect.client is PySpark's, of Apache Spark as it is: of no __all__, it imports * of core and the getLogLevel of pyspark.sql.connect.logging. So its names, of dir() and of from pyspark.sql.connect.client import *, are PySpark's, those classes, getLogLevel and the modules core and retries, but for PySpark's modules artifact and reattach, which the transport replaces, and for retries until it is imported (by get_retry_policies, set_retry_policies, a retry_policy of SparkConnectClient, or an import of it), as it imports grpc: until then the package has no attribute retries, which PySpark's core imports. core defines PySpark's names, PYSPARK_ROOT, _is_pyspark_source and _import_zstandard_if_available too, and the private helpers of the drop-in. Of the names that PySpark's core imports, it has those that it imports too, such as logger and os, and those of retries (RetryPolicy, Retrying, DefaultPolicy and DEFAULT_MAX_RETRY_EXCEPTION_ELAPSED_TIME) once they are read, which its dir() does not list, but not the others, such as grpc, pd and ArtifactManager. The package and core need none of pandas, PyArrow, grpc and protobuf, which PySpark's core imports, and import without them (see dev/parity/known-differences.md). The functions of pyspark.sql.connect.functions are of its modules (builtin and partitioning), and so are those of pyspark.sql.connect.avro.functions and pyspark.sql.connect.protobuf.functions: they are not those of pyspark.sql.functions, pyspark.sql.avro.functions and pyspark.sql.protobuf.functions, as in PySpark. An alias, such as column, negate, power or random, is the function col, negative, pow or rand, of that name, as PySpark binds it.

pyspark.sql.utils is PySpark's module, of Apache Spark as it is, of its names and its helpers: is_remote() and is_remote_only() are True, and its decorators, such as try_remote_functions and dispatch_df_method, run the functions of PySpark Connect's modules of their names, and the methods of the classes of Spark Connect, which an object of another class does not have (NOT_IMPLEMENTED). The package pyspark.sql.connect has the names of PySpark's, check_dependencies and utils, which its __init__ imports, and importing pyspark imports no module of it, as in PySpark: the functions of pyspark.sql.functions, PySpark's, import pyspark.sql.connect.functions when one of them is first called. Its import does not run check_dependencies, which PySpark's does, nor does the import of pyspark.ml.connect, which has the name too, as PySpark's (see dev/parity/known-differences.md).

pyspark.sql.SparkSession is PySpark's classic class, the module pyspark.sql.session of Apache Spark as it is, as in PySpark. Its builder reads spark.remote or SPARK_REMOTE, raises CONNECT_URL_NOT_SET without either, also while a session is active, and makes the session with the builder of pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession, of which the session is. So isinstance(spark, pyspark.sql.SparkSession) is False, as in PySpark, and active() and getActiveSession() of the classic class give the session of Spark Connect. The builder of pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession, of a classproperty of pyspark.sql.session, is PySpark Connect's: it does not read SPARK_REMOTE, raises SESSION_NEED_CONN_STR_OR_BUILDER without a URL or a channel builder, returns the active session from getOrCreate, and its enableHiveSupport raises NOT_IMPLEMENTED, where that of the classic builder sets spark.sql.catalogImplementation.

The classic classes of pyspark.sql.conf, pyspark.sql.tvf, pyspark.sql.datasource, pyspark.sql.merge, pyspark.sql.observation, pyspark.sql.catalog, pyspark.sql.readwriter, pyspark.sql.udf, pyspark.sql.udtf, pyspark.sql.group, pyspark.sql.pandas.group_ops, pyspark.sql.streaming.readwriter and pyspark.sql.streaming.query are PySpark's, of those modules of Apache Spark as they are, which pyspark.sql and pyspark.sql.streaming name as PySpark's do. So isinstance against them is False, as in PySpark, of a session's conf, tvf, dataSource, catalog, read, readStream, streams, udf and udtf, of a DataFrame's mergeInto, write, writeTo, writeStream, groupBy and cogroup, of a StreamingQuery and of the UDTFs above. Their constructors and methods are those of Spark Classic, as PySpark's: pyspark.sql.DataFrameReader(spark) and pyspark.sql.Catalog(spark) raise the JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED of _jsparkSession, and so does the register of a pyspark.sql.udf.UDFRegistration(spark), as in PySpark, where the reader of spark.read and pyspark.sql.connect.readwriter.DataFrameReader(spark) are PySpark Connect's. Observation(...) makes an Observation of pyspark.sql.connect.observation, which is not an instance of pyspark.sql.Observation, as PySpark's __new__ makes one. pyspark.sql.connect.window.Window is a subclass of pyspark.sql.window.Window, as in PySpark, of PySpark Connect's code.

The classic Column, DataFrameNaFunctions, DataFrameStatFunctions, Window, WindowSpec, TableArg and TableValuedFunctionArgument are PySpark's classes, of their modules and MROs (pyspark.sql.column and pyspark.sql.table_arg of Apache Spark as they are), which pyspark.sql names as PySpark's does. Their Connect classes, which the objects of a session are of, are native, and a native class cannot have a Python base, so they are their virtual subclasses, as the DataFrame is of the public pyspark.sql.DataFrame: isinstance and issubclass hold as in PySpark, while the MRO of such an object is its native class and object, where PySpark's has the classic class and its bases after its Connect class. The explicit calls of the classic methods dispatch as PySpark's (Column.alias(col, "x") runs the Connect class's, and of another object it raises NOT_IMPLEMENTED), the classic Column(...) and WindowSpec(...) raise the ModuleNotFoundError of pyspark.sql.classic, and the others construct and subclass as PySpark's plain classes do. A patch of a classic class or of TableValuedFunctionArgument, such as a method that a library sets on pyspark.sql.Column, reaches the objects of a session as it reaches PySpark's Connect objects, which inherit it: not where the Connect class has the name itself, nor where the objects set it on themselves (_expr of a Column, df of na) and the patch is not a data descriptor; deleting it gives the native class its own attribute back. What stays different: these classic classes are of an ABCMeta subclass, of an _abc_impl among their attributes, and a class that subclasses one of them is of abc.ABCMeta, where PySpark's are of type; and of a data descriptor without a setter patched over such an attribute of the objects, PySpark's __init__ of a Connect object raises its AttributeError, where the drop-in's object reads the patch. The readers and writers of PySpark Connect are subclasses of the OptionUtils of pyspark.sql.connect.readwriter, a class of private methods only, of which the drop-in's native readers and writers are not: their MRO is their class and object, and pyspark.sql.connect.readwriter has no OptionUtils.

PySpark's classes are plain Python classes, which a user subclasses. So are these of the drop-in: the DataFrame, Observation, and the SparkSession, Catalog, DataSourceRegistration, DataFrameReader and DataStreamReader of pyspark.sql.connect, which construct of their PySpark arguments (SparkSession(connection=...), Catalog(spark), DataFrameReader(spark)), also a subclass of an __init__ of its own, and whose setters, copies and pickles are of the subclass (but those of a session, which are the active session of its ID, as PySpark's); SparkSession.Hook, StorageLevel and PythonEvalType; and the data types, from StringType and DecimalType to ArrayType, StructField and StructType (see above). A session of a subclass is the session that its DataFrames, readers and catalogs give back, as in PySpark. The __init__ of the class gives an object its session, as PySpark's __init__ sets it: the session of a new client, of SparkSession(connection, userId=None, hook_factories=None), and the session of its argument for the others, which must be a session, where PySpark's keeps any object until it is used, which raises its AttributeError then. Until it runs, as for a subclass whose __init__ does not call it, a session, a reader or a catalog is of a session of no server, whose requests raise NO_ACTIVE_SESSION, where PySpark's raise the AttributeError of the first attribute that the method reads: _client of a session, _sparkSession of a catalog, and _options, _schema or _format of a reader (a reader or a catalog is of the first session among the arguments of a subclass, if any, which then works), and a registration has no sparkSession, as PySpark's. So a pickle of PySpark, which makes an object of its class without arguments and then sets its __dict__, loads in the drop-in: a reader, of the _client, _format, _schema and _options (and _source_name) of its state, which it sets as its setters do, a catalog of its _sparkSession and a registration of its sparkSession; and the drop-in's pickles of them load in PySpark, of their classes, as PySpark's own do: where the session of their ID is active. The other native classes, of which the Connect Column, DataFrameNaFunctions, DataFrameStatFunctions, WindowSpec and TableArg are, cannot be subclassed (TypeError: type 'Column' is not an acceptable base type), and do not construct (TypeError: cannot create '...' instances): their objects are made of the state of the Rust core, a plan, an expression or a query, which the arguments of PySpark's constructors, the Python objects of its client, do not give, as the drop-in does not have them, so a subclass would have no __init__ to call: - Column takes an Expression of pyspark.sql.connect.expressions; the drop-in's expressions are the Rust core's. - DataFrameWriter, DataFrameWriterV2, DataStreamWriter and MergeIntoWriter take the LogicalPlan of a DataFrame, which the drop-in's _plan stands in for. - GroupedData and PandasCogroupedOps take a DataFrame and the expressions of its grouping, of the plan of the Rust core. - DataFrameNaFunctions and DataFrameStatFunctions take a DataFrame, of whose native plan they are. - WindowSpec takes the expressions of its partitioning and ordering and a WindowFrame, and TableArg a SubqueryExpression, of the plan of the Rust core. A WindowSpec has PySpark's _partitionSpec, _orderSpec and _frame as properties of the native object, not in its __dict__: lists of the _expr of Columns, whose repr is that of PySpark's expressions ([a], [a ASC NULLS FIRST]), made at each read, and the WindowFrame of pyspark.sql.connect.window, or None. - RuntimeConf takes a SparkConnectClient, whose transport is native. - StreamingQueryManager and StreamingQuery take a session and the IDs of a query, of the listener bus and the queries of the Rust core. - TableValuedFunction takes a session, of whose native core it is.

A copy.copy or copy.deepcopy of a DataFrame requests its schema as PySpark's does, one request for the copy, and one more for the DataFrame in a deep copy when it has no schema yet, so a stopped session fails the copy with SparkConnectException, as PySpark's does. One difference remains: PySpark's DataFrame.__getattr__ answers getattr(df, "__deepcopy__") and getattr(df, "__copy__") by requesting the schema, to read the columns, and raises ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED, so hasattr(df, "__copy__") is false; the drop-in defines both itself, which it finds without a request. An unpickled DataFrame requests its schema once, at the unpickle, which raises the error of the request or of its conversion, as PySpark's pickle looks the __setstate__ of the new DataFrame up through its __getattr__. Its cached schema is then that of the pickled DataFrame, as the state of PySpark's pickle sets it, of the objects that it carries: of none, its schema requests it again. So does the unpickle of an object that PySpark pickles with its DataFrame: a writer, of its callback, grouped data, na and stat; a stream writer, which PySpark's pickles of the plan of the DataFrame, requests nothing.

A copy, a deep copy or an unpickle of a DataFrame keeps the schema that it requests apart from the cached schema of the state, as PySpark's keeps it as the _cached_schema_serialized that its schema returns. So the two differ when the schema on the server changed since the DataFrame cached it, such as that of a view that was replaced, and the copy gives, as PySpark's, the schema that it requested for schema, printSchema, toArrow, the set operations of equal cached schemas (c.union(c).schema) and the numeric aggregations of its grouped data (sum() of no columns), and the cached schema for columns, dtypes, repr, the column lookups and the methods that copy the cached schema, such as filter. A copy of such a copy keeps the schema that its own reconstruction requests, and the cached schema, which a pickle of it carries too. Of a DataFrame that had no cached schema, both give the schema of the server, which the next read of the copy requests again.

to caches its schema whatever it is, as the object that it is, as PySpark's, so of a DataType that is not a struct, such as LongType(), schema gives a copy of it without a request, while its plan is sent, which the server rejects; and of a StructType changed in place after the call, schema, columns and the plan that the requests send are of the type as it is then. The methods that copy the cached schema of their input in PySpark copy that of to too: alias, filter and where, limit, sort, orderBy and sortWithinPartitions, hint, repartition, repartitionByRange, repartitionById and coalesce, distinct and dropDuplicates, sample, randomSplit and observe, as do the set operations of equal ones.

The other objects of a session above, a streaming query and the Connect builder, pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession.builder, keep the attributes that are set on them through copies and pickles, as PySpark's copy and pickle their __dict__: a shallow copy shares them, and a deep copy, a pickle and cloudpickle copy them, where they copy the object at all. Where PySpark's fail, the drop-in's fail with the same errors, such as the AttributeError of the creator of the session of a plain pickle of spark.streams, and the TypeError of its lock of a deep copy and of cloudpickle. Their __dict__ holds only those attributes, where PySpark's holds the state of the object too, as the _options of a builder. A shallow copy of the builder of pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession shares its options and its hook factories all the same, as PySpark's copy shares its _options dict and its _hook_factories list: a remote, a config or a _registerHook of either one is seen by both, while a channelBuilder sets the channel builder of the one that it is called on, as it rebinds an attribute of PySpark's.

A table name that is neither a str nor bytes, and bytes that are not UTF-8, give a DataFrame of read.table, readStream.table and changes, whose plan raises protobuf's TypeError or the decode error when it is built, as PySpark's do. A reader's format that is not a str is kept as the object it is, which _format gives back, and a copy or a pickle of the reader keeps it. The Connect builder's remote keeps a value that is not a str as PySpark's does, and create rejects it as an invalid Spark Connect URL, as PySpark's create does for its str(). An explicit None, given as remote(None), remote(location=None) or config("spark.remote", None), is kept as None: create and getOrCreate fail PySpark's assertion, unless a session exists, which getOrCreate returns. A later remote replaces it. A remote() without an argument is sc://localhost, as in PySpark's Connect builder. The locks are PySpark's: getOrCreate holds SparkSession._lock from its lookup to the options that it sets, create to make its session the default one, and stop() throughout, and the builder holds SparkSession.Builder._lock in config, remote, appName, channelBuilder and _registerHook, and while it sets the options of a session. Each is a class attribute, an RLock, read at each call, so a thread of the program that holds one holds off the calls of the other threads that take it, and a signal ends the wait for it. As PySpark's, getOrCreate sets the options of a session that it creates twice, in create and again.

The client honors the HTTP proxy of the environment (grpc_proxy, https_proxy, http_proxy, no_grpc_proxy, no_proxy) with grpcio's rules, see HTTP Proxies, with two differences: a loopback host is never proxied, where grpcio proxies localhost unless no_proxy lists it, and a proxy address with an invalid host or port is the error of the creation of a session of a host that the proxy applies to, where grpcio makes the session and fails its requests, but for a port past 65535, which it takes modulo 65536 and connects to (a proxy of port 99999 is reached at 34463): the error names the variable at once, rather than requests that fail later or a connection to a port that was not given. A host that no_proxy lists connects directly whatever that address, as in grpcio, which resolves it only for a host that it proxies. As grpcio, the client logs a proxy variable that is not a proxy, and a roots file that cannot be read, as errors on stderr (see Errors on stderr).

As grpcio's, a channel connects to the addresses of its host, or of its proxy, as the system's resolver gives them, within the connect deadline, but those of localhost and of the names under it, the loopback of both families, as c-ares, grpcio's resolver, gives them (::1, then 127.0.0.1): to the first, then to each next one 250 ms after the previous one, or at once once the previous one failed, while none is done, each with a connect deadline of 20 s of its own, which its TCP connection, the tunnel of the proxy, the TLS handshake and the HTTP/2 settings that the server sends first share. The first to complete is the connection, and the others are dropped. The connection is the process's: the sessions of the same server, proxy, TLS and keepalive, and of no token, share it, as gRPC's global subchannel pool shares the subchannels of PySpark's channels, so a session of newSession(), cloneSession() or the clone of a client, and any other session of the same connection string, uses the connection of its session, while each reads the variables of the proxy again, as grpcio's channel of a new client does; a session of a token has a connection of its own, also of newSession() and cloneSession(), as grpcio's channels of the credentials of a token, of each session, share none. The window of a connection is the largest of HTTP/2, so that the results that a session holds open and does not read on, as of toLocalIterator(), do not hold the calls of the other sessions of the connection, nor its other calls, as gRPC's connections, whose windows grow with those of their streams; the window of each stream, of 2 MiB, bounds what it holds unread. A child of os.fork() makes the threads, the runtime and the channels of the client again, as grpcio's fork support does, so that its sessions, and those of its parent, run queries there, and leaves those of its parent to the parent: a session of the parent that the child frees or stops leaves the connection of its channel to the parent, which reads it on, and an execution of the parent that the child drops is not released. The child closes the sockets of the connections of its parent and the epoll instances of its parent's runtime as the fork returns, as grpcio's fork support closes the descriptors of the event engine of a parent, so that a connection of the parent ends on the server with the parent; the eventfd of its parent's runtime stays, an eventfd of the child's own, which an object of the parent writes to when it wakes a task of that runtime, one descriptor of each generation (see dev/parity/known-differences.md). The client writes the lines of gRPC's core to stderr without the lock of Rust's stderr, and the state that its threads keep is of each generation or read without a lock, so that a lock that a thread of the parent held at the fork does not hold the child. A fork while another thread makes a call can leave the child waiting, as grpcio's fork support asks that no other thread makes a call then, and so can a fork while the client makes a call in the background (a release of an execution, the removal of a cached relation or of a model, the events of the streaming query listeners), which holds the lock of the hooks, the user context extensions, the plan compression or the last execution of its session for the moment that it reads them, and so can a fork while a thread of the client releases a Python object without the GIL, as of a retry policy, whose release PyO3 defers under a lock of its own, which the next call of the child into the client waits for. The tags and the user context extensions of the other threads of the parent stay in the child, which never forgets them, as those threads end in the parent only: a leak bounded by the threads of the parent.
