A message over the size limit of a call, 128 MiB, as PySpark's channel sets grpc.max_receive_message_length and grpc.max_send_message_length, fails the call with grpcio's RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, of the details of gRPC's core: Stream removed (CLIENT: Received message larger than max (<length> vs. <limit>)) of a response, and CLIENT: Sent message larger than max (<length> vs. <limit>) of a request, which is not sent. So does the metadata of a response, its headers or its trailers, past gRPC's limits of the metadata that a call receives, of HPACK's sizes of its entries: at 16 KiB (grpc.absolute_max_metadata_size), Stream removed (received metadata size exceeds hard limit (value length <length> vs. 16384)) of an entry too large alone, or (<size> vs. 16384); <entries>, at once, also of metadata far larger, where the drop-in failed with INTERNAL (transport error) or retried an UNAVAILABLE of the end of its connection; and past 8 KiB (grpc.max_metadata_size), at random, the more often the larger it is, of soft limit, of the entries as gRPC's core lists them. The connection advertises the hard limit as the size of a header list that it takes, as grpcio's channel does, so that Spark's server, of grpc-java, resets the stream of a call whose metadata would reach it, as an error whose message has a few hundred CJK characters gives, of grpcio's INTERNAL, Stream removed (RST_STREAM (Received RST_STREAM with error code 1)), where the drop-in raised the hard limit of the metadata that it received; a stream that a server resets fails so of the code of the reason, as gRPC's core gives it. Past the soft limit, the call still has the details of the server's error, as grpcio's call does, and its failure is PySpark's ValueError of grpc_status, Code in Status proto (StatusCode.INTERNAL) doesn't match status code (StatusCode.RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED), where it was the SparkConnectGrpcException of RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: as PySpark reads the google.rpc.Status of each failure with rpc_status.from_call, the failure of a status that its details do not match, of their code or of their message, is that ValueError, raised as grpcio's error of the call is handled (its __context__), of no log of the error where the DefaultPolicy or the iterator of a reattachable execution reads it, and after GRPC Error received where _handle_rpc_error does (see dev/parity/known-differences.md), of no context where the DefaultPolicy reads it before a retry, as PySpark's Retrying does between its attempts. So is the failure of a grpc-status-details-bin that gRPC's core does not decode as base64: as gRPC's core, the client fails the call INTERNAL of the details Stream removed (Error parsing 'grpc-status-details-bin' metadata: illegal base64 encoding), whatever the code of the server, and gives it the status details empty, a status of the code OK (Code in Status proto (StatusCode.OK) doesn't match status code (StatusCode.INTERNAL)). Of details of base64 that upb's parser, PySpark's protobuf, does not read as a google.rpc.Status, as of one nested past its limit (see above), of a string that is not UTF-8 (String field had bad UTF-8) or of a tag of more than five bytes, the failure is protobuf's DecodeError, as PySpark's rpc_status.from_call raises it, while a field that the type knows of another wire type is read as one that it does not know, as upb reads it; and so is the failure of a status whose first ErrorInfo, which _handle_rpc_error unpacks, or first RetryInfo, which the DefaultPolicy unpacks, upb does not read (Error parsing message with type 'google.rpc.ErrorInfo': Wire format was corrupt), where PySpark unpacks it. The first detail of a type is the first that protobuf's Any.Is tells of it, of a type URL of a /, of any host, and the metadata of an ErrorInfo holds the entries that upb sets in its map, not those of a field that the entry type does not know or of a key or a value of another wire type. As PySpark's convert_exception, the classes and the messageParameters of the metadata are parsed with Python's json.loads, of the values of the JSON as they are, and its error is the failure, as the JSONDecodeError of JSON that does not parse, of grpcio's error as its context (or as that of the StopIteration of json that it suppresses); the errorClass of the metadata, also empty, is the condition. The delay of a RetryInfo is PySpark's, the ToMilliseconds() of its retry_delay, signed and unbounded and 0 of one of none, which the log gives as it is, and so is the wait before a retry, of Python's numbers, which a negative delay never lengthens. A negative wait, and one of decades, are slept of Python's time.sleep, as PySpark's Retrying sleeps them, which raises at once, of no context, of one that it cannot hold: its ValueError of a negative one (sleep length must be non-negative), its OverflowError of one past its nanoseconds of 64 bits (timestamp out of range for platform time_t from Python 3.11 on), or the system's OSError of one that the clock cannot hold. A signal that comes while it sleeps ends the wait as one that comes during any other wait of the call: its KeyboardInterrupt interrupts the execution in flight. A request sent in the background sleeps it on a thread of Python of its own, and fails of its error, which is logged as PySpark's sender logs it (ReleaseExecute failed with exception: ...). A policy that PySpark's Retrying decides, as a subclass of DefaultPolicy, is asked of a failure as grpcio's error of the call is handled, as PySpark's AttemptManager asks it, so that what its can_retry raises has that error as its context. A channel that cannot connect fails its calls with UNAVAILABLE, which the retry policy retries, of the last error of its addresses: of a plaintext server that accepts the connection and never answers, grpcio's failed to connect to all addresses; last error: UNKNOWN: ipv4:127.0.0.1:15002: connection attempt timed out before receiving SETTINGS frame. Once it failed, it fails the later calls at once, of that error, while it connects again in the background with gRPC's backoff, 1 s and then 1.6 times longer each time up to 120 s, with a jitter of 20 %, each attempt with the longer of its backoff and 20 s as its deadline, until a connection succeeds, which the next call takes; once no call came for 30 min, or once every session of the connection is stopped, it stops, and the next call connects, as grpcio's channel goes idle, or shuts down. A connection that ends is made again by the next call. The Python client logs the failures of the connections that gRPC's core logs, on stderr (see Errors on stderr), and its CONNECT request of a proxy has grpcio's User-Agent: grpc-httpcli/0.0. What stays different, such as the keepalive pings, which are hyper's, is in dev/parity/known-differences.md.

The user agent, <user_agent> spark/4.3.0 os/<os> python/<version> of the version of Python, as PySpark's ChannelBuilder.userAgent makes it, is sent as PySpark sends it: as the client type of the requests that PySpark builds with it, and not as a header. The user-agent header is the client library's own, tonic/<version> here and grpcio's in PySpark, such as grpc-python/1.85.1 grpc-c/58.0.0 (linux; chttp2). A user-agent parameter of the connection string is checked as metadata and not sent, as grpcio replaces it with its own. So a user agent may hold any character, a control character included. As PySpark's userAgent, which its requests read when they are built, a user agent longer than 2048 characters after URL escaping, or a SPARK_CONNECT_USER_AGENT that is not UTF-8, is the error of each request that carries it, which is not sent: SparkConnectException, or the UnicodeEncodeError of urllib.parse.quote. The session is made all the same, its stop() logs the error as that of its release, and the requests that PySpark builds without the user agent, of the artifacts and of CloneSession, are sent. As urllib.parse.urlsplit does, a tab, CR or LF anywhere in the connection string is removed. SPARK_CONNECT_USER_AGENT is read as each call of the client starts, so that a change of os.environ applies to the next call, as PySpark's requests read the variable when each is built, and a request that the transport builds during a call, such as a reattachment or a release in the background, has the user agent of the last call that started.

A gRPC failure whose status carries no error of the server, such as of an unreachable server or of a proxy, is the SparkConnectGrpcException of its code whose message is the text of grpcio's error of the call, as PySpark's _handle_rpc_error raises it: <_InactiveRpcError of RPC that terminated with:, or <_MultiThreadedRendezvous for ExecutePlan and ReattachExecute, and the lines of its code (status = StatusCode.UNAVAILABLE), its details and its debug_error_string, as grpcio 1.85 gives them. The message of a call past its deadline begins with that text, as PySpark's f"{error}: RPC deadline exceeded. ...", and that of a status of a google.rpc.Status without an ErrorInfo is the message of the status. The details are the message of a status that the server sent, and the debug_error_string is the name of the code and the details, as in grpcio. Those of a failure that the client detects itself are those of gRPC's C core: of a channel that cannot connect, failed to connect to all addresses; last error: UNKNOWN: ipv4:127.0.0.1:1: Failed to connect to remote host: Connection refused, of the last error of its addresses, such as a TLS handshake of BoringSSL's error or a proxy that refuses the tunnel (HTTP proxy returned response code 403), of a name that does not resolve, errors resolving ..., and of a call that the end of its connection fails, Stream removed (Socket closed). The errors of copyFromLocalToFs and cloneSession, which PySpark leaves to grpc, are grpcio's RpcError, as there (see SparkSession.client).

As PySpark's Retrying, a call whose retries of a failure that a policy retries are spent warns [RETRIES_EXCEEDED] The maximum number of retries has been exceeded. before it raises the failure: a UserWarning of the location of PySpark's warnings.warn in pyspark.sql.connect.client.retries, and of that module, which its filters and the actions of a location take as PySpark's, and which a filter of "error" raises in place of the failure. So do the lookup of the plan compression of the first plan of a session, whose failure is caught, the read of the conf of the server's stack trace as an error of the server is raised, which is retried as PySpark's, and the release of the session of stop(). A policy retries the failures that its can_retry takes, as PySpark's Retrying asks it, also a subclass of RetryPolicy that is not a DefaultPolicy, and warns when its retries are spent; policies none of which takes a failure, such as PySpark's own RetryPolicy, retry nothing, and do not warn. The requests that the client sends in the background, which no caller waits for, warn too, and their failures are logged as PySpark's senders log them (ReleaseExecute failed with exception: ...), from the delivery thread of the drop-in (see dev/parity/known-differences.md). stop() logs the failure of the release of its session to the logger of Spark Connect (pyspark.sql.connect.logging), which is disabled unless SPARK_CONNECT_LOG_LEVEL is set, as PySpark's: session.stop(): Session could not be released. Error: $<error>.

With SPARK_CONNECT_LOG_LEVEL, the client logs to the logger of Spark Connect what PySpark's client logs of its RPCs, of the same levels and messages: the deadlines of a new client (Spark Connect RPC deadlines: ...), each retry and the end of the retries of a call (Given up on retrying. error: ...), and each gRPC failure that it converts (GRPC Error received, of grpcio's RpcError, and Received ErrorInfo: ... of an error of the server). The debug logs of its plans and of their responses are not (see dev/parity/known-differences.md).

For TLS roots, including GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH, see TLS Root Certificates.

docs.title: Native NaiveBayes
docs.text:
The Rust ml::NaiveBayes and ml::NaiveBayesModel train and predict through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. The Rust-backed Python API exports NaiveBayes from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.classification; fit returns the typed NaiveBayesModel, whose transform produces DataFrame predictions.

All nine PySpark constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, labelCol, predictionCol, probabilityCol, rawPredictionCol, smoothing, modelType, thresholds and weightCol. Rust exposes corresponding builder setters and getters. Unset parameters are omitted so the server uses its defaults. The Python constructor is keyword-only and converts values with PySpark's parameter converters.

All four model types are covered by live tests: multinomial, bernoulli, complement and gaussian. Multinomial/complement inputs must be nonnegative; Bernoulli inputs must be binary; Gaussian inputs may contain continuous negative values. Tests also cover multiclass dense/sparse inputs, probability/raw score columns, smoothing and instance weights, threshold decisions, suppressed vector outputs, independent fits, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. A golden fixture captures all nine parameters for each model type from official PySpark.

The Rust NaiveBayesModel has PySpark 4.3.0's model members: pi, theta and sigma (a 0 by 0 matrix for multinomial, complement and Bernoulli models), numClasses, numFeatures, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of one vector, and NaiveBayesModel::load. NaiveBayes::load reads a saved estimator with one ML Read, as PySpark's NaiveBayes.load does. The estimator's fit returns this typed model. PySpark 4.3.0 gives the model no training summary. The Rust param accessors are generated from PySpark's param table: features_col and set_features_col replace the former feature_col and set_feature_col.

In Python, NaiveBayes and its NaiveBayesModel follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, pi, theta, sigma, numClasses, numFeatures, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of a vector, and save and load. A NaiveBayes model has no training summary, as in PySpark. The vendored pyspark.ml.classification API continues to use its existing implementation.

docs.title: Native BisectingKMeans
docs.text:
The Rust ml::BisectingKMeans and ml::BisectingKMeansModel support training and DataFrame cluster assignment through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. Python exports the native estimator from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns its BisectingKMeansModel.

All eight constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, predictionCol, maxIter, seed, k, minDivisibleClusterSize, distanceMeasure and weightCol. Rust also provides parameter getters. The keyword-only Python constructor matches official PySpark's order/defaults and parameter conversions. Unset parameters are omitted so the server uses its defaults, including k=4.

Live tests cover hierarchical splitting, absolute/fractional minimum divisible cluster sizes (which may produce fewer than k leaves), instance weights, Euclidean/cosine distance, sparse/dense inputs, seeded reproducibility, independent fits, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. Golden fixtures compare all eight parameters at six signed seed/integer-width boundaries with official PySpark.

The Rust model's members, summaries and persistence are in "Native clustering models (Rust API)". In Python, BisectingKMeans, its BisectingKMeansModel and BisectingKMeansSummary follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, clusterCenters(), computeCost(dataset), numFeatures, predict of a vector, the training summary (k, clusterSizes, trainingCost, numIter, predictions and cluster, of the transform of the training dataset, as PySpark's), and save and load. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API is unchanged.

docs.title: Native GeneralizedLinearRegression
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::GeneralizedLinearRegression fits Spark's JVM estimator and returns a cached GeneralizedLinearRegressionModel. Python exposes it from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.regression; fit returns its GeneralizedLinearRegressionModel.

All 16 PySpark constructor parameters and named setters are available: labelCol, featuresCol, predictionCol, family, link, fitIntercept, maxIter, tol, regParam, weightCol, solver, linkPredictionCol, variancePower, linkPower, offsetCol and aggregationDepth. Rust provides builder setters and getters for each parameter. Unset optional parameters stay unset: Spark chooses the family default link, or the Tweedie link power from variancePower.

Fitting accepts ML vector features and numeric labels. Transform produces predictions and, when requested, the linear predictor in linkPredictionCol. Instance weights, offsets and L2 regularization are handled by Spark. The same numerical tests run against official PySpark and the native Python client, covering all five families (Gaussian, binomial, Poisson, Gamma and Tweedie), default and explicit links, dense/sparse features, weights, offsets, independent fitted models, lazy model ownership and rejected inputs. Official PySpark golden fixtures verify the parameter encoding, and live Rust tests exercise fitting and prediction directly.

The Rust model's members and persistence are in "Native regression models (Rust API)". In Python, GeneralizedLinearRegression, its GeneralizedLinearRegressionModel, GeneralizedLinearRegressionSummary and GeneralizedLinearRegressionTrainingSummary follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, coefficients, intercept, numFeatures, predict of a vector, the training summary (of the training dataset, as PySpark's, with residuals(residualsType) and the statistics of the coefficients), evaluate, and save and load. As PySpark's over Spark Connect, residuals sends its positional arguments only: residuals(residualsType="pearson") gives the deviance residuals. As with PySpark, the repr of a model whose link is not set fails on the server.

docs.title: Native GaussianMixture
docs.text:
Rust ml::GaussianMixture and ml::GaussianMixtureModel train Gaussian mixture models and produce cluster assignments and component probabilities through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. Python exports the native estimator from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns its GaussianMixtureModel.

All nine constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, predictionCol, k, probabilityCol, tol, maxIter, seed, aggregationDepth and weightCol. Rust also provides corresponding getters. The keyword-only Python constructor matches official PySpark's order/defaults and conversions. Unset values are omitted so the server uses its defaults.

Live tests cover one- and two-dimensional mixtures, two/three components, normalized probabilities and assignments, dense/sparse vectors, weights, seeded reproducibility, independent fits, disabled probability output, server validation, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. Golden fixtures compare all nine parameters at six signed seed/integer-width boundaries with official PySpark.

The Rust model's members, summaries and persistence are in "Native clustering models (Rust API)". In Python, GaussianMixture, its GaussianMixtureModel and GaussianMixtureSummary follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, weights, gaussiansDF, gaussians (a MultivariateGaussian of each collected row of gaussiansDF, as PySpark builds them), numFeatures, predict and predictProbability of a vector, the training summary (probability, probabilityCol, logLikelihood and the members of a clustering summary, of the transform of the training dataset, as PySpark's), and save and load. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API is unchanged.

docs.title: Native FMClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::FMClassifier and pyspark.ml.connect.classification.FMClassifier fit Spark's binary factorization machine classifier. The 17 parameters of PySpark's constructor have Rust builder setters and getters and named Python setters; weightCol, a param of the class that PySpark's constructor does not take and that PySpark has no setter of, has a Rust getter only. Fitted models produce prediction, probability and raw-prediction columns, with configurable thresholds. Both the gd and adamW solvers run on the Spark server.

The Rust FMClassificationModel has factors, linear, intercept, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of one vector, numClasses, numFeatures, and load. FMClassifier::load reads a saved estimator with one ML Read, as PySpark's FMClassifier.load does. Its summary() is the binary training summary of a fitted model, and has_summary() says whether one exists; summary() fails for a loaded model, as PySpark does. evaluate(&df) returns the binary summary of a DataFrame, with the ROC, PR and threshold DataFrames.

In Python, FMClassifier, its FMClassificationModel and their summaries follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, factors, linear, intercept, numClasses, numFeatures, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of a vector, summary() (the training summary: objectiveHistory, totalIterations, roc, pr and the other curves), evaluate, and save and load.

docs.title: Native MultilayerPerceptronClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::MultilayerPerceptronClassifier and its native Python binding support the 14 params of PySpark's class: the 13 of its keyword-only constructor, and thresholds, which the constructor does not take, as PySpark's does not, and which setThresholds (set_thresholds in Rust) sets. Configure layers before fitting; input and output sizes must match the feature dimension and number of classes. initialWeights accepts dense or sparse ML vectors: Rust uses MlVector (a Vec<f64> or array also converts to a dense vector), and Python accepts the values supported by PySpark's TypeConverters.toVector. Layer arrays and vector parameters are encoded in Rust and checked against fixtures captured with official PySpark.

The fitted model produces multiclass prediction, probability and raw-prediction columns. Both l-bfgs and gd are supported. As in PySpark, fitting an empty DataFrame can return a model; the native client preserves that server behavior.

The Rust MultilayerPerceptronClassificationModel has weights, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of one vector, numClasses, numFeatures, and load. MultilayerPerceptronClassifier::load reads a saved estimator with one ML Read, as PySpark's MultilayerPerceptronClassifier.load does. Its summary() is the multiclass training summary of a fitted model, and has_summary() says whether one exists. summary() fails for a loaded model, as PySpark does. evaluate(&df) returns the summary of a DataFrame. The param accessors are generated from PySpark's param table.

In Python, MultilayerPerceptronClassifier, its MultilayerPerceptronClassificationModel and their summaries follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, weights, numClasses, numFeatures, predict, predictRaw and predictProbability of a vector, summary() (the training summary: objectiveHistory and totalIterations), evaluate, and save and load.

docs.title: Native OneVsRest
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::OneVsRest and pyspark.ml.connect.classification.OneVsRest implement the multiclass reduction in Rust. Supply a native binary classifier, for example OneVsRest::new().set_classifier(LinearSVC::new()) in Rust or OneVsRest(classifier=LinearSVC()) in Python. The Classifier enum accepts all eight native binary classifiers: LogisticRegression, LinearSVC, DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier, NaiveBayes, FMClassifier and MultilayerPerceptronClassifier. Perceptron base classifiers need a two-unit output layer.

In Python, the classifier can be any other object, as in PySpark. The native fit is that of a classifier of exactly a native class. Any other classifier, such as PySpark's own classes of pyspark.ml.classification, or a Python subclass of them or of a native class, is fit by PySpark's own OneVsRest._fit over the estimator's params, which runs the classifier's own fit and _fit for each class (classifier.fit(trainingDataset, paramMap)), overrides of a subclass too. Its model is PySpark's OneVsRestModel of the classifier's own models. A None classifier is fit there too, and fails at its first use. So is a dataset that is not a Spark DataFrame: a pandas DataFrame raises the KeyError of PySpark's pandas aggregate of its max label.

All seven PySpark constructor parameters have named setters. Rust exposes scalar parameter getters and the configured classifier. Fits clone the base classifier for each class and run at most parallelism fits at once. Python observes mutations to the supplied classifier made before fit, while fitting leaves that classifier unchanged. Instance weights are forwarded to each class's fit when the base classifier is a HasWeightCol of PySpark, which every native classifier is but the perceptron (FMClassifier included). For the perceptron, Python warns weightCol is ignored, as it is not supported by <uid> now., with the classifier's uid, as PySpark does, and fits without the weights. The warning is attributed as PySpark's is, to the line of its warnings.warn in pyspark/ml/classification.py and to the module pyspark.ml.classification, whose filters match it.

A fit runs the steps of PySpark's OneVsRest._fit, in its order and of its requests, in Rust and in Python, but for the reads of each class's model that PySpark's makes after its fit (numClasses of a LogisticRegression model), which the Rust API makes when they are asked for:

  • Classes: the fit reads the max label first, as dataset.agg({labelCol: "max"}).head()["max(" + labelCol + ")"]: the max of the label column as named, which the server resolves (a name with a dot names a field of a struct), of the column's own type. The classes are int(max) + 1, of Python's int, so the max of a string column is its greatest string (labels "10", "9" and "0" fit ten classes, and the rows of "10" are of no class), a fraction is truncated (a max of -0.5 fits one class), and a null (of no rows), a NaN, an infinity or a string that is no integer raises the TypeError, ValueError or OverflowError of int. Python takes PySpark's own Python values and int. Rust converts the max as int does, of the same messages, but of the ASCII digits of a string only, where Python's int takes the decimal digits of other scripts too.
  • Dataset: the label, features and weight columns (dataset.select(labelCol, featuresCol, weightCol)) are cached while the classes fit when the input is not persisted, as PySpark's _cache_spark_dataset(..., StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK) caches them: persisted, and unpersisted after the fits and the reads of their models; or, with SPARKML_TEMP_DFS_PATH set, saved under that path, read back, and deleted after by the ML helper (handleOverwrite). The binary label of each class is 1.0 where the label column of that dataset (multiclassLabeled[labelCol]) is the class, and the training summary of each class's model is of its binary training set.
  • Pool: then PySpark makes its list of the tasks of the classes and its pool of min(parallelism, classes) threads, so that a parallelism below one, a null one, and a max label below zero raise their errors after the max label is read and the dataset is cached: ValueError: Number of processes must be at least 1, or the TypeError of min of a None. This client fits at most 2147483647 classes: a count beyond raises a MemoryError in Python (and an error in Rust), where PySpark allocates its list of that many tasks ([trainSingleClass] * numClasses, of 8 bytes a class, 16 GiB of 2^31 classes, before any fit), and beyond 2^63 the OverflowError of that list, as PySpark's.
  • Params: the params are read where PySpark reads them, with no check of their own: an unset classifier raises PySpark's KeyError of the param, a null labelCol the AttributeError of F.col(None), a null featuresCol the TypeError of the select (after the max query), a null predictionCol is sent to the classifier's fits, which the server rejects, and a null rawPredictionCol fits, as PySpark's does. In Python, parallelism is an int of any size, which PySpark compares and never sends, and which saves and loads as it is.

The model aggregates the positive-class raw scores of its submodels into rawPrediction and chooses the first highest score for prediction, ignoring NaN/null scores as PySpark does; it produces no probability column. In Python, transform is PySpark's own OneVsRestModel._transform, and the Rust transform is a port of it, with the same DataFrame operations and so the same requests. Each submodel transforms the data with its own featuresCol and rawPredictionCol, not the model's, so a model whose featuresCol names no column still transforms, and a model rawPredictionCol that the submodels do not produce fails with UNRESOLVED_COLUMN when the transform is evaluated, as PySpark's does. The scores are accumulated in a mbc$acc<uuid> column. When the input is not persisted, the transform persists it at MEMORY_AND_DISK while it builds the composition and unpersists it then, as PySpark's _cache_spark_dataset does. With SPARKML_TEMP_DFS_PATH set, a copy of the input is written there and read back, and the copy is deleted before the transform returns: as in PySpark, the returned DataFrame then fails with PATH_NOT_FOUND when it is evaluated. Temporary columns and fit-created caches are cleaned up, and transformed DataFrames retain the binary models for lazy evaluation. Models must transform data in their fitting session.

Rust OneVsRest::fit returns the typed OneVsRestModel. Its models() gives each binary submodel as its typed model, one SubModel variant per native classifier, and classifier() gives the classifier. Single-vector prediction is on the submodels. OneVsRestModel::new(session, models) constructs a model of the given models, of a new uid and no set params or classifier, as PySpark's OneVsRestModel(models), and its set_classifier sets the classifier.

Persistence is of PySpark's Python format, in Rust and in Python, as PySpark's OneVsRestWriter, OneVsRestModelWriter and their readers write it: OneVsRest::write().save(path) and OneVsRest::load(session, path), and the same for OneVsRestModel. The metadata of the estimator has its params without the classifier, which is saved at classifier, in the order of the maps of the Python object that it saves, as PySpark's extractJsonParams writes them (of the constructor's defaults of a OneVsRest of its constructor, of the names of a load or a copy); the metadata of the model also has numClasses, and each submodel is saved at model_<index> by its own writer. What each of PySpark and this client saves, the other loads, with the same uids, params and predictions, and the metadata files equal PySpark's apart from their timestamps and uids (of a subclass, of its class, see "Subclasses" above). As PySpark's readers, the loads read metadata of any class, of PySpark's Python format and of the JVM's class names, which classic PySpark's JavaMLWriter (and Scala's writer) saves of a OneVsRest of a Java classifier, in the same layout, also as a stage of a pipeline. A load of a model loads its classifier and each of its models once, of PySpark's requests. A CrossValidator or a TrainValidationSplit over a OneVsRest saves and loads with it, and a param map of the validator sets the params of the classifier, as PySpark's copy does. In Rust, a param map of a model sets the params of its models (apply_param_map), as PySpark's OneVsRestModel.copy(extra) copies each model with it.

In Python, the OneVsRest estimator has the Params API of pyspark.ml (its classifier param included), setClassifier, fitMultiple and clear, and its fit returns the typed OneVsRestModel, which has classifier, the other params, transform, and a uid of its own, as PySpark's. OneVsRestModel(models) constructs a model of the given models, of a new uid and the defaults of the class, with no set params and no classifier, as PySpark's constructor does, and its models attribute can be assigned. Its models are the typed submodels, each with the uid of the classifier, the binary label of its class as labelCol, the classifier's params, and its training summary. They are made from the fitted submodels without a request, each of the typed model class of its classifier. A LogisticRegression submodel is a typed LogisticRegressionModel, with its training summary; a DecisionTreeClassification submodel is a typed DecisionTreeClassificationModel; a RandomForestClassification submodel is a typed RandomForestClassificationModel with its training summary (binary, as its class's fit is); and a GBTClassification submodel is a typed GBTClassificationModel, with the trees of its ensemble. The per-class fits send the requests of PySpark's, and PySpark's client also reads the post-fit requests of each submodel: numClasses of a LogisticRegression submodel, and numClasses and trees of a RandomForestClassification one, and trees of a GBTClassification one. PySpark's makes the reads of a class right after its fit, on the thread of its pool that fits it (its try_remote_fit), so they come between the fits of the classes; this client's core fits the classes, in the threads of its own pool, and then the Python client makes the reads of each class, in their order, once all the fits are done: the requests are the same, of another order. Their order would need a Python call of each class's fit on the threads of the core's pool, for no other difference.

As PySpark's, the write() of a OneVsRest or a OneVsRestModel gives its writer, whose save raises the KeyError of the unset classifier param of one of no classifier (a OneVsRestModel of its constructor too), and then PySpark's ValueError of validateParams of a classifier or a submodel that is not writable (OneVsRest write will fail because it contains ... which is not writable.), before any request.

docs.title: Native AFTSurvivalRegression, IsotonicRegression and FMRegressor
docs.text:
All eight regression estimators in PySpark 4.3.0 now have native Rust fit/transform implementations. The three additions are available under spark_connect::ml and pyspark.ml.connect.regression, and are re-exported from pyspark.ml.connect. They fit Spark's JVM estimators and retain the returned server-cached models for as long as a model clone or transformed DataFrame needs them.

  • AFTSurvivalRegression fits a Weibull accelerated failure time model. It accepts positive survival times and a censor column (1 for observed events, 0 for censored observations), and can produce a vector of requested quantiles. All 11 constructor parameters have Rust and Python setters, including quantileProbabilities, quantilesCol, and the aggregation/block-size settings.
  • IsotonicRegression fits increasing or decreasing univariate regression. It supports scalar features or a selected vector component (featureIndex), instance weights, interpolation between fitted boundaries, and clamping beyond the training range. All six constructor parameters have setters.
  • FMRegressor fits factorization machines with pairwise interactions and optional intercept and linear terms, using either adamW or gd. All 14 constructor parameters have setters, including factor size, initialization, mini-batch fraction, regularization and seed.

Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. The Python wrappers preserve PySpark's keyword-only constructor signatures and type conversion, and take ML vector features, as pyspark.ml's do.

The Rust models' members and persistence are in "Native regression models (Rust API)". In Python, the three estimators and their models follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, numFeatures and predict, coefficients, intercept, scale and predictQuantiles of a survival model, boundaries and predictions of an isotonic model, whose predict takes a single feature value, intercept, linear and factors of an FM model, and save and load.

Parameter goldens come from official PySpark 4.3.0. Native Rust and Python tests exercise censoring and quantiles, weighted isotonic interpolation, both FM solvers, validation errors and cached-model lifetimes. The Python behavior tests also run unchanged against the official client.

docs.title: Native LDA and PowerIterationClustering
docs.text:
The native Rust and Python APIs now implement all five clustering algorithms in PySpark 4.3.0: KMeans, BisectingKMeans, GaussianMixture, LDA and PowerIterationClustering. The Rust models' members and persistence are in "Native clustering models (Rust API)".

Rust ml::LDA supports online and EM training and cached-model DataFrame transforms. Python exposes LDA through pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns a DistributedLDAModel of the em optimizer and a LocalLDAModel of the online one, as PySpark's. All 14 constructor parameters have Python setters and Rust builder setters/getters, including document/topic concentrations, learning settings, checkpoint settings, seed and topic-distribution output column. Both optimizers return a vector of topic probabilities per document; empty documents produce zero vectors. As with pyspark.ml, an array feature column is sent as it is, and the JVM rejects one whose elements may be null, such as the arrays of createDataFrame.

ml::PowerIterationClustering::assign_clusters and Python assignClusters build Spark Connect's powerIterationClusteringAssignClusters helper relation. This algorithm has no fit/transform API or fitted model. It accepts source/destination vertex columns and optional nonnegative edge weights, with k, maxIter and initMode settings, and returns a Spark DataFrame with id: bigint and cluster: int. Parameter values are captured when the relation is built. Omitting weightCol uses unweighted edges; an explicit null remains distinct from an omitted parameter and is validated by Spark. The lazy relation retains any cached models used by its input DataFrame.

Both APIs require Spark DataFrames and reject pandas inputs. Reference-derived golden fixtures and live tests cover both LDA optimizers, dense/sparse inputs, graph initialization modes, weighted/unweighted graphs, custom columns, setters, validation and model lifetime. The Rust models' members and persistence are in "Native clustering models (Rust API)". In Python, LDA, LDAModel, LocalLDAModel and DistributedLDAModel follow the full API of pyspark.ml (see "Native ML classes of the full pyspark.ml API"): the Params API, the members of an LDA model (describeTopics, topicsMatrix, logLikelihood, logPerplexity, vocabSize, isDistributed and estimatedDocConcentration; describeTopics sends its positional arguments only, as PySpark's over Spark Connect, so describeTopics(maxTermsPerTopic=1) describes the server's 10 terms), toLocal (the same LocalLDAModel on every call, as PySpark's, of the constructor of its class), trainingLogLikelihood, logPrior and getCheckpointFiles of a distributed model, and save and load. PowerIterationClustering has its uid and the Params API, and saves and loads as PySpark's does: as the params of the server's PowerIterationClusteringWrapper. LDAModel is the base class of the two LDA models, as PySpark's, with the members of an LDA model but no persistence of its own: an LDA model is an instance of it, LDAModel.load is an AttributeError, and a copy or a load of a model is of the model's class. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API is unchanged.

docs.title: Native feature stages
docs.text:
All 38 standard pyspark.ml.feature estimators and transformers have native Rust execution and Python bindings. Rust exposes them as spark_connect::ml::<Name>, with typed builder setters/getters. Python exports them from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.feature, with standard pyspark.ml.feature keyword-only constructor signatures and named mutating setters. The vendored pyspark.ml.feature module is unchanged.

Area Stages Text and categorical features CountVectorizer, HashingTF, IDF, Word2Vec, Tokenizer, RegexTokenizer, NGram, StopWordsRemover, StringIndexer, IndexToString, OneHotEncoder, TargetEncoder, FeatureHasher Scaling and numeric transforms StandardScaler, MaxAbsScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler, Normalizer, Binarizer, Bucketizer, QuantileDiscretizer, Imputer, DCT, PolynomialExpansion, ElementwiseProduct Assembly and selection VectorAssembler, VectorIndexer, VectorSizeHint, VectorSlicer, Interaction, PCA, ChiSqSelector, UnivariateFeatureSelector, VarianceThresholdSelector, RFormula, SQLTransformer Locality-sensitive hashing BucketedRandomProjectionLSH, MinHashLSH

The 18 transformers build lazy ML relations, and the 20 estimators fit through Spark Connect's ML command. In Python each is a typed class with PySpark's Params API (params, getParam, the getters and setters, copy, extractParamMap), write/save/read/load; the estimators also have fitMultiple. A transformer's transform, and an estimator's fit, apply a non-empty param map to a copy as PySpark does. HashingTF.indexOf fails at PySpark's JVM import, as the official one does over Spark Connect. The outputCol default of a loaded stage is the one of the object that its load makes (<a new uid>__output), not of the saved uid, as PySpark's load keeps the defaults of that object when it takes the saved uid (_resetUid). A fit returns one of 19 typed model classes, with PySpark's members: getters and setters, attributes such as mean, vocabulary, pc and categoryMaps, DataFrames such as surrogateDF, approxNearestNeighbors, approxSimilarityJoin, getVectors and findSynonyms, and the class methods CountVectorizerModel.from_vocabulary and StringIndexerModel.from_labels and from_arrays_of_labels. Over Spark Connect, PySpark's relation decorator (try_remote_attribute_relation) drops every keyword argument of approxNearestNeighbors, approxSimilarityJoin, getVectors and findSynonyms, and ours does too, as PySpark's behavior over Spark Connect: a distCol given by keyword is ignored (the column stays distCol), and a call whose positional arguments are not all given, or of more (getVectors(1)), fails at the server, as official's does. The class methods take their arguments in PySpark's order: an empty vocabulary raises the ValueError of from_vocabulary (of its len) first; then the model of the class's constructor gets the object that the ML helper builds of its uid and of list(...) of the labels of any iterable (a str, a set, the keys of a dict), sent as PySpark's serialize sends them ((list(labels), ArrayType(StringType())) of from_labels, whose literal asserts each string), after the assertion of an active session; and then the setters of the given params, whose TypeConverters raise their TypeError after the request. QuantileDiscretizer's fit returns a Bucketizer of a new uid, with its splits and its input and output columns, of its keyword constructor, as PySpark's _create_model does, and of the defaults of the discretizer that _copyValues gives it (an outputCol of the discretizer's uid). Transformed DataFrames retain their fitted models and upstream input plans. The Rust wrapper of the discretizer's splits is named QuantileDiscretizerModel. Training-only parameters are omitted from model transforms. Multi-column parameters, nested Bucketizer splits, vector-valued ElementwiseProduct weights, NaN imputation values, and UnivariateFeatureSelector's setter-only parameters are supported. RegexTokenizer's gaps, which has no converter in PySpark, keeps its Python value, which a transform and a save send as its literal (of LiteralExpression._from_value, as PySpark's serialize_param), so that a load has it; a value of no literal raises its error at either.

StandardScaler and MaxAbsScaler exports now refer to the native implementations. This changes the previous deprecated pyspark.ml.connect scaler behavior: pandas frames and array-valued feature columns are rejected; transforms return Spark DataFrames containing vectors. Mean centering is opt-in through withMean=True. Convert pandas data with spark.createDataFrame and array columns with array_to_vector before fitting.

This covers constructor parameters, named setters, fit and DataFrame transform, and StopWordsRemover.loadDefaultStopWords, which reads the server's default stop words through Spark Connect's ML helper, as PySpark does (Rust StopWordsRemover::load_default_stop_words). As PySpark's constructor does, StopWordsRemover() fetches its default locale and then its English stop words of the active session, once each, so without one it raises PySpark's bare AssertionError. They are the defaults of PySpark's own __init__ (_setDefault), which the native stage takes, so a load sends its Read and then these two requests, and a copy sends none, as PySpark's. The Rust StopWordsRemover::load sends its Read alone, where PySpark's load also fetches these two defaults, in the constructor of the loaded stage: only the requests differ, since a Rust stage, new or loaded, reads an unset locale or stop_words as None or empty and the server applies its defaults.

In Rust, each fitted model also has the members of its PySpark model class, which it reads of the server-side model as PySpark does: for example CountVectorizerModel::vocabulary, PCAModel::pc, the scaler statistics, VectorIndexerModel::category_maps, the LSH models' approx_nearest_neighbors and approx_similarity_join, and Word2VecModel::get_vectors and find_synonyms. CountVectorizerModel::from_vocabulary and StringIndexerModel::from_labels and from_arrays_of_labels build a model of given values, and QuantileDiscretizer::fit_bucketizer gives the Bucketizer of the fitted splits, as PySpark's fit does. Every stage and model saves with write() and loads with load(session, path), as PySpark's save and load. Pipeline/tuning execution is separate from this native surface. Existing vendored helper classes remain available.

Tests compare all 38 stages with official PySpark 4.3.0 parameter literals and Spark results, including 10 multi-column/parameter variants, both constructor and setter configuration, model lifetime, invalid inputs and pandas rejection. Schema checks compare class identifiers, nullability and ML metadata; Connect omits the backing SQL schema of JVM UDTs on the wire. Run scripts/capture_ml_features_golden.py with the official client to regenerate the fixture. scripts/capture_feature_models_golden.py captures the members of every fitted model, the class methods, and the save and load of every stage, which e2e_feature_models.rs compares. Native live tests run in CI; set FEATURE_REFERENCE=1 explicitly to run their reference mode. They also check that every feature object that this client makes (a stage, its copy and load, a fit and the copy and load of its model, the models of the class methods) is of the class of its module, and that the Pipeline of pyspark.ml fits, saves and loads the stages.

docs.title: Native FPGrowth and PrefixSpan
docs.text:
Rust ml::FPGrowth fits Spark's frequent-itemset model and returns a typed FPGrowthModel. The model exposes lazy freq_itemsets() and association_rules() DataFrames and transform() predictions. The Python classes are exported from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.fpm; fitted models expose freqItemsets and associationRules as properties. All five estimator constructor parameters have named setters; model setters cover the item column, prediction column and minimum confidence. Parameters for prediction are captured when its lazy plan is built. The itemset/rule properties fetch the fitted server model, matching standard PySpark's Connect attribute relations.

The Python FPGrowth and FPGrowthModel follow pyspark.ml.fpm in full: the Params API (params, getParam, extractParamMap, explainParams, copy, set, clear, Param objects and getters), setParams and fitMultiple of the estimator, and write, save, read and load of both. A fitted model copies its estimator's defaults, as PySpark's _copyValues does. PrefixSpan has the same Params API, and no persistence, as Spark has none.

Rust ml::PrefixSpan::find_frequent_sequential_patterns and Python PrefixSpan.findFrequentSequentialPatterns mine arrays of itemsets directly through the Connect helper, with all four constructor parameters and named setters. They return sequence/frequency DataFrames and have no fit/transform model.

These APIs accept Spark DataFrames and reject pandas frames before requests; a dataset that is not a DataFrame is sent as PySpark sends it (see the argument rules above). Lazy model tables retain their cached model; PrefixSpan retains its input plan, including any upstream fitted models. A fitted model's transform of a DataFrame of another session is lazy and fails with CONNECT_ML.CACHE_INVALID when the result is analyzed or collected, as PySpark's does. In Rust, FPGrowth and FPGrowthModel save with write() and load with load(session, path), as PySpark's save and load. The vendored pyspark.ml.fpm module is unchanged.

Spark 4.3.0's Connect helper currently rejects Long argument literals: PrefixSpan's maxLocalProjDBSize works within the signed 32-bit range, including its default 32,000,000; larger values raise the same LONG not supported server error as official PySpark. The client preserves PySpark's integer widths and explicit null parameters. Tests cover this limitation, typed string/integer itemsets, association rules, held-out predictions, model setters, sequence-length limits, invalid data, and model lifetime.

docs.title: Native ALS recommendation
docs.text:
ml::ALS / ml::ALSModel in Rust and pyspark.ml.connect.recommendation.ALS / ALSModel in the Rust-backed Python package run Spark's standard ALS over Connect. The estimator exposes all 18 parameters, including explicit/implicit feedback, nonnegative factors, regularization, block counts, storage levels and seed. Python mirrors the 17 official constructor keywords; use setPredictionCol for an alternate prediction column, and setNumBlocks to set both block counts.

The fitted model supports transform, rank, user/item factor tables, recommendations for all users/items, and recommendations for a subset of users/items. Rust uses user_factors, item_factors, and recommend_for_*; Python exposes userFactors, itemFactors, and recommendFor*. Model setters control transform parameters, including coldStartStrategy="drop" to remove predictions for unknown IDs. Factor and recommendation relations access the fitted server model, matching PySpark Connect. Lazy results retain their cached model and any models referenced by the subset DataFrame until evaluation completes.

The Python ALS and ALSModel follow pyspark.ml.recommendation in full: the Params API, getters and setters, setParams, setNumBlocks, fitMultiple, copy, and write, save, read and load. A model's coldStartStrategy, userCol, itemCol and blockSize come from its estimator, as _copyValues gives them. The rank of a model is read from the server on each access, as PySpark's _call_java("rank") does, so a load sends no request for it. PySpark's fit also fetches it once, or twice when rank is set, as its _copyValues probes hasParam("rank") of the new model and so reads that property; the Python and Rust fits do not, so only the requests differ.

Fit, transform and subset recommendation inputs must be Spark DataFrames; pandas DataFrames are rejected before conversion or RPC, and a subset's other values are sent for the server to reject, as PySpark sends them. Model operations must use the fit session for transforms: another session's DataFrame fails with CONNECT_ML.CACHE_INVALID when the transform is analyzed or collected, as PySpark's does. The subset recommendations accept another session's DataFrame and run, as PySpark's do. Official PySpark 4.3.0 fixtures cover explicit and implicit ratings, predictions, cold starts, factors, and all four recommendation methods, with live Rust and native Python tests. In Rust, ALS and ALSModel save with write() and load with load(session, path), and a loaded model reads its rank of the server, as PySpark's does. Live tests also check that the CrossValidator and TrainValidationSplit of pyspark.ml fit, save and load an ALS with a native RegressionEvaluator.

docs.title: Native ML evaluators
docs.text:
Rust and the Rust-backed pyspark.ml.connect.evaluation exports provide all six standard Spark ML evaluators: regression, binary classification, multiclass classification, multilabel classification, clustering and ranking. Their constructor parameters and named setters follow pyspark.ml.evaluation in PySpark 4.3.0. Rust also provides typed parameter getters. Metric direction is available as is_larger_better() / isLargerBetter() without contacting Spark. pyspark.ml.connect.evaluation also exports PySpark's own pyspark.ml.evaluation.Evaluator, the base class of the six, so that it has the names of pyspark.ml.evaluation (as pyspark.ml.connect.tuning exports PySpark's ParamGridBuilder), while the Evaluator, Estimator, Transformer and Model of the pyspark.ml.connect package stay the deprecated classes of pyspark.ml.connect.base, as in PySpark's deprecated package.

The three evaluators of upstream's deprecated pyspark.ml.connect.evaluation (regression, binary and multiclass classification), which the native classes of this module replace, use standard Spark ML defaults: BinaryClassificationEvaluator takes rawPredictionCol="rawPrediction", and MulticlassClassificationEvaluator defaults to metricName="f1" and requires keyword arguments. Use rawPredictionCol / setRawPredictionCol instead of the deprecated probabilityCol / setProbabilityCol binary-evaluator argument.

Evaluation sends Spark DataFrames and their column names/types directly to Spark. A pandas DataFrame raises the AttributeError of its own sparkSession, as pyspark.ml does, before serialization or RPC; a model's summary evaluate raises the TypeError of pyspark.ml instead. Prepare double prediction columns, vector scores, and arrays of doubles where required by the corresponding standard evaluator. Clustering features may be vectors or arrays of doubles. Evaluators no longer silently cast columns, convert array scores to vectors, or normalize field-name casing.

Official PySpark fixtures and live Rust/Python tests cover every supported metric, weights, regression through the origin, binary score bins, multiclass log-loss clipping and beta, per-label metrics, both silhouette distances, ranking cutoffs, invalid inputs, and metric direction. In Rust, each evaluator saves with write() and loads with load(session, path), as PySpark's, and set_uid sets its uid, as PySpark's _resetUid does. In Python, each evaluator has PySpark's Params API, its getters and setters, setParams, and write/save/read/load, which keep its uid and params. evaluate(dataset, params) with a non-empty param map evaluates a copy of the evaluator, as PySpark's Evaluator.evaluate does, and leaves the evaluator as it was. scripts/capture_evaluation_api_cases_golden.py captures these cases from official PySpark.

scripts/capture_fpm_recommendation_evaluation_golden.py captures the members of the FPGrowth and ALS models and of the evaluators, and their save and load, of the configurations of these fixtures, which e2e_fpm_recommendation_evaluation.rs compares.

docs.title: Native ML statistics
docs.text:
Rust's ml::{ChiSquareTest, Correlation, KolmogorovSmirnovTest, Summarizer, SummaryBuilder, MultivariateGaussian} and the native Python classes in pyspark.ml.stat cover the standard ML statistics APIs from PySpark 4.3.0. The Python module is a Rust-backed shim, replacing its vendored implementation, except MultivariateGaussian, which stays PySpark's plain Python class. pyspark.ml.connect adds no statistics module; its summarizer is the one of PySpark's deprecated package, unchanged.

The module has PySpark's names and no __all__, as PySpark's, so from pyspark.ml.stat import * imports the same names (the names of its imports too, such as Column and JavaWrapper). ChiSquareTest, Correlation, KolmogorovSmirnovTest and Summarizer construct as PySpark's plain classes: of no arguments (ChiSquareTest() takes no arguments) unless a subclass has an __init__ of its own, of attributes and weak references, and pickled and copied as plain objects. SummaryBuilder is a JavaWrapper of PySpark's __init__(self, jSummaryBuilder), which keeps no Java object over Spark Connect: its summary reads the _metrics of its attributes, which Summarizer.metrics sets with a _java_obj of None, so SummaryBuilder(None).summary(col) raises PySpark's AttributeError, and a subclass that sets _metrics summarizes of them. The classes have PySpark's docstrings, and their static methods (and SummaryBuilder.summary) are functions of the module of PySpark's signatures, annotations and docstrings (Summarizer.mean.__module__ is pyspark.ml.stat, and its docstring has the .. versionadded:: 2.4.0 of PySpark's since), over the native methods, so inspect and help give PySpark's and a call binds as PySpark's does (SummaryBuilder.summary() takes from 2 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given); Summarizer._check_param and _get_single_metric are PySpark's code over Spark Connect. The annotations name PySpark's classic Column of pyspark.sql.column, as PySpark's do, of which the Columns of a session are instances, and the classes are subclasses of the native classes, which their MROs name after them (ChiSquareTest, ChiSquareTest, object), where PySpark's are plain classes.

The statistical tests return lazy Spark DataFrames. Chi-square supports both the vector result and one row per feature (flatten=True); correlation supports Pearson and Spearman; the KS test supports Spark's normal distribution, with optional mean and standard deviation. Spark validates column types and statistical arguments. As with pyspark.ml.stat, the dataset and the other arguments are serialized as the arguments of a helper call, in that order, before any RPC: a pandas DataFrame raises PySpark's UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE, and another argument that cannot be a literal raises the error of its conversion. A literal of another type than the helper takes, such as a dataset that is not a DataFrame or a column name that is not a str, is sent as PySpark sends it, and the server rejects it when the result is analyzed or collected (tests/golden/statistics_arguments.json records these cases of official PySpark). A (value, DataType) pair is sent as the literal of that type, as PySpark sends it, and raises the AssertionError of PySpark's LiteralExpression(value, dataType) of a value or type that a literal does not take. The KS test converts its parameters with float() first, as PySpark does. Results retain any fitted models used by their input plans.

Summarizer.metrics(...).summary(features, weight) builds a SQL aggregate that works in select and grouped aggregations. All ten metrics are supported: mean, sum, variance, std, count, numNonZeros, max, min, normL1, and normL2. Each also has a static convenience method; Rust uses snake_case (num_non_zeros, norm_l1, norm_l2). Omitted weights default to 1.0. Inputs are ML vector Columns, including sparse vectors. Metric names are case sensitive; numNonZeros uses a capital Z. An empty metric selection returns an empty struct.

MultivariateGaussian is a mutable mean/covariance holder, with no computation or extra validation. Rust uses MlVector and MlMatrix (dense or sparse storage, the matrix type of the native ML params). Python keeps PySpark's plain class, whose instances hold the original vector and matrix objects and pickle as PySpark's. Python results materialize vectors and matrices through the existing ML UDT conversion.

Reference protobuf fixtures and live Rust/Python tests cover every metric with and without weights, grouped summaries, chi-square flattening, both correlation methods, KS parameters, constant-feature NaNs, invalid inputs, and lazy model ownership. Python tests additionally compare sparse and dense inputs. Native classes are asserted explicitly; the tests also run separately with official PySpark as the reference.

docs.title: Configuration and Connection
docs.text: Configure connections to local or remote Spark Connect servers, set session parameters, and manage authentication.

docs.title: Connection String Format
docs.text:
Connection strings follow the format sc://host:port/;param=value. Parameters are optional:

Parameter Purpose Example token Authentication token, sent over TLS to any host but localhost sc://host:15002/;token=abc123 user_id User identity sc://host:15002/;user_id=alice session_id Session identifier sc://host:15002/;session_id=sess_xyz use_ssl Enable TLS sc://host:15002/;use_ssl=true

Note

TLS and authentication parameters are passed in the connection string. Consult your infrastructure team for any required credentials or certificates.

docs.title: Building a Session
docs.text:
use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

// Session configuration is applied at runtime via `spark.conf()`:
spark.conf().set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "20")?;

docs.title: Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
Access and modify session configuration at runtime:

// Get a config value
let partitions = spark.conf().get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions")?;

// Set a config value
spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")?;

docs.title: Starting a Local Spark Connect Server
docs.text:
To run a Spark Connect server locally for development:

# Set SPARK_HOME to your Spark installation
export SPARK_HOME=/path/to/spark

# Start the server on sc://localhost:15002
$SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh

The Spark distribution bundles the Spark Connect server, so it needs no --packages.

The server listens on port 15002 by default. To use a different port, add --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.port=<port>.

Tip

The Spark Connect server requires a JVM and Apache Spark 4.3.0 or later. Stop it with $SPARK_HOME/sbin/stop-connect-server.sh.

docs.title: Remote Connections
docs.text:
To connect to a remote Spark Connect server:

use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://spark.example.com:15002/;token=YOUR_TOKEN")
    .get_or_create()?;

Replace spark.example.com, the port, and authentication parameters as needed. As in PySpark, a token implies TLS, so this connects over TLS. A token of the SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN environment variable does the same. Only to localhost is a token sent without TLS, for local development; to 127.0.0.1 and [::1] it is sent over TLS, as in PySpark. Without a token, use_ssl=true turns TLS on:

use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://spark.example.com:15002/;use_ssl=true")
    .get_or_create()?;

docs.title: HTTP Proxies
docs.text:
As PySpark's client (through grpcio), the client reaches the server through the HTTP proxy of the environment, with an HTTP/1.1 CONNECT tunnel. TLS is negotiated with the Spark server inside the tunnel and checked against the server's name, so the proxy sees neither the token nor the data. As grpcio, the client connects to the addresses of the proxy as to those of a server, the next one 250 ms after the previous one, each with a connect deadline of 20 s, and its CONNECT request carries the Host and, of a proxy URI with a user, the Proxy-Authorization headers, and of the Python client grpcio's User-Agent: grpc-httpcli/0.0 too.

export https_proxy=http://user:password@proxy.example.com:3128
export no_proxy=.internal.example.com,10.0.0.0/8

The proxy is the first of grpc_proxy, https_proxy and http_proxy that is set, and the hosts that are not proxied are those of no_grpc_proxy, or else of no_proxy. These are the rules of grpcio:

  • Only the lowercase names are read; HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are not.
  • Only an http:// proxy is supported. Another scheme (https://, socks5://), a value without a scheme or an empty one connects directly. An invalid value is logged as an error of each session, whatever its host (see Errors on stderr).
  • The user and password of the proxy URI, percent-decoded, are sent as Proxy-Authorization: Basic. A proxy without a port is on port 443.
  • A no_proxy entry matches the host itself or its subdomains (example.com and .example.com both match spark.example.com, not notexample.com), and an IP host in a CIDR range such as 10.0.0.0/8. There is no * wildcard, and an entry with a port does not match.

Unlike grpcio, a loopback host (localhost and the names under .localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, [::1], and IPv4-mapped loopback addresses) is never proxied: its traffic need not leave the machine, and a token is sent to localhost without TLS. A proxy address with an invalid host or port is an error when a session of a host that the proxy applies to is created, where grpcio makes the session and fails its requests, as it cannot resolve the address, or takes a port past 65535 modulo 65536 and connects to that port: the error names the variable at once, rather than requests that fail later or a connection to a port that was not given. As in grpcio, which resolves the address of the proxy only for a host that it proxies, a host that no_proxy lists, as a loopback host, connects directly whatever that address. A value that is not UTF-8 is not used, and the client connects directly, where grpcio reads its bytes.

docs.title: TLS Root Certificates
docs.text:
A TLS channel trusts the root certificates of the system's trust store, which SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR can replace, and, of the Python client where grpcio is installed (PySpark's retry policies need it), those of grpcio's own bundle too, the roots.pem of the installed grpc package, which grpcio's channels trust by default. As in grpcio, GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH names a PEM file whose certificates are trusted instead, such as the CA of a corporate proxy that inspects TLS:

export GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH=/etc/ssl/corporate-ca.pem

The file replaces the other roots rather than adding to them. As in grpcio, the variable and the file are read once, when the first TLS session of the process is made, and an empty file is as no file. A file that cannot be read is logged as an error (see Errors on stderr), and the client uses the default roots. A file without a certificate does not fail the session when it is made, as in grpcio: each call fails UNAVAILABLE, Failed to create security handshaker., and so does each call of a system without roots, where neither grpcio nor a file gives some.

The Python client trusts more than PySpark does, on purpose: a CA of the system's trust store, such as the private CA of a company that its administrators install, is trusted, which PySpark, of grpcio's bundle alone, does not trust. So a program whose server has such a CA keeps connecting when grpcio is installed as a dependency of another package, and every server that PySpark's client trusts is trusted. The Rust API takes the system's store rather than a bundle of its own as it holds the CAs that the administrator of the machine installs, and is kept up to date with the system rather than with the releases of the client.

docs.title: Errors on stderr
docs.text:
PySpark's own code says nothing of a proxy variable that is not a proxy, of a roots file that cannot be read, of a TLS handshake that fails or of a proxy that refuses the tunnel: gRPC's C core, in grpcio, logs them to stderr, the failure of a TLS handshake as information (I) and the others as errors (E). The Python client logs them there as lines of the same form, which name the Rust source of the call, where grpcio's name its own:

E1118 16:53:41.241267 4026384 http_proxy_mapper.cc:<line>] 'https' scheme not supported in proxy URI
E1118 17:37:31.168823  299507 proxy.rs:<line>] the 'https' scheme of the proxy URI is not supported in https_proxy; not using a proxy
I1119 01:06:45.505781 3300774 ssl_transport_security.cc:<line>] Handshake failed with error SSL_ERROR_SSL: error:1000007d:SSL routines:OPENSSL_internal:CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: unable to get local issuer certificate
I1119 02:15:41.966502  505468 connector.rs:<line>] Handshake failed with error SSL_ERROR_SSL: error:1000007d:SSL routines:OPENSSL_internal:CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: unable to get local issuer certificate
E1119 01:03:42.670473 3254142 http_connect_client_handshaker.cc:<line>] HTTP proxy handshake with ipv4:127.0.0.1:3128 failed: UNKNOWN: HTTP proxy returned response code 403
E1119 02:15:42.060818  505955 connector.rs:<line>] HTTP proxy handshake with ipv4:127.0.0.1:3128 failed: UNKNOWN: HTTP proxy returned response code 403

The <line> is the line of the source file that logs it.

As in grpcio, a proxy variable is logged for each session that is connected, once for a session of newSession() and of cloneSession() too, whose channel reads it again, the roots file once, when it is read, a TLS handshake that fails at each attempt to connect, in the background too, and a tunnel that fails once a minute at most, whatever the attempts in between, as gRPC's core limits the line of its source. Nothing is logged when GRPC_VERBOSITY is NONE as the client is imported, and only the errors when it is ERROR, as grpcio reads it when it initializes; of INFO or DEBUG, the client logs what it logs by default, without the other lines that gRPC's core logs then. The Rust API gives the errors of the variables and of the roots file to tracing, as warnings; the failures of its connections are in the errors of its calls.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. This is an Apache Software Foundation project, so a few conventions apply.

The repository holds the Rust client crates under crates/ and the Python drop-in: the pyspark package under python/pyspark, around the pyspark._pyspark extension that the crates/pyspark-rs crate builds. Architecture shows how they fit together.

docs.title: Issues and discussion
docs.text: Bugs and feature requests are tracked in ASF JIRA under the SPARK project - GitHub Issues are disabled. Reference the JIRA key in your pull request title, e.g. [SPARK-XXXXX][CONNECT] Short summary, with [PYTHON] after [CONNECT] for a change to the Python drop-in.

docs.title: Building and testing
docs.text:
Requires a Rust toolchain and protobuf-compiler. Non-Windows aarch64 builds also need the target C tools described in the source build requirements.

cargo build                 # build the library crates
cargo test                  # unit + golden-proto tests
cargo build -p examples     # the Rust-native examples

Builder correctness is covered by golden-proto tests: plans, expressions, all SQL functions, the reads, the catalog calls and ML transforms are asserted byte-for-byte against captured reference protos. The goldens under tests/golden/ are captured from the official pyspark-client by the scripts/capture_*_golden.py scripts, against a Spark Connect server: run each with that client's Python, isolated, as python -I scripts/capture_golden.py --remote sc://localhost:15002. Transport and Arrow paths are exercised by the end-to-end tests below and by the official Apache Spark Connect test suite in CI - see the CI notes under dev/design/.

The end-to-end tests (crates/spark-connect/tests/e2e_*.rs and a few others) run only when SPARK_REMOTE names a Spark Connect server; without it they pass without checking anything. They share one server session, so CI runs them on one thread:

SPARK_REMOTE=sc://localhost:15002 \
  cargo test -p apache-spark-connect --test e2e_dataframe -- --test-threads=1

The wasm-udf example crates need the wasm32 target and are built by manifest path (they're excluded from the workspace):

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --manifest-path examples/wasm-udf-inline/Cargo.toml

docs.title: A local Spark Connect server
docs.text:
The end-to-end tests, the live Python tests and the official test suites run against a Spark 4.3.0 Connect server. The Spark distribution bundles the server, so no --packages is needed: unpack spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect.tgz (the one CI uses) or spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3.tgz from the Apache CDN, which serves the current releases, or the Apache archive, which keeps every release but is slower. scripts/download_spark_dist.sh 4.3.0 spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect DIR downloads and unpacks it as CI does, from the CDN or else from the archive. Start it with Java 17 and CI's settings:

export SPARK_HOME=/path/to/spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect
(cd "$SPARK_HOME" && TZ=UTC SPARK_TESTING=1 PYSPARK_PYTHON="$(command -v python)" \
  ./sbin/start-connect-server.sh \
  --driver-memory 3g --conf spark.sql.session.localRelationSizeLimit=1073741824)

It listens on sc://localhost:15002 and logs to $SPARK_HOME/logs; stop it with "$SPARK_HOME"/sbin/stop-connect-server.sh. The settings:

  • TZ=UTC makes UTC the session time zone, as on CI's runners. The test commands below set it too.
  • SPARK_TESTING=1 turns on Spark's test-mode defaults, which some tests rely on.
  • PYSPARK_PYTHON is the Python that runs UDFs on the server. It needs pandas and pyarrow, and the same minor version as the Python that runs the tests, or their UDFs fail with PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH. Start the server with the virtual environment active.
  • Starting it from $SPARK_HOME lets the official tests' relative data paths resolve.

docs.title: Python drop-in
docs.text: python/pyspark holds Rust-backed shims over pyspark._pyspark and code vendored from PySpark (see below). Its tests assert the behavior of official PySpark 4.3.0: where the two differ, PySpark is the reference (see Compatibility).

docs.title: Set up Python
docs.text:
The package supports Python 3.9 or later (requires-python in pyproject.toml); CI runs Python 3.11. Create a virtual environment with the packages CI installs. pandas stays below 3.0, which PySpark 4.3 does not fully support yet:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install pytest coverage 'pandas>=2.2,<3.0' pyarrow numpy grpcio grpcio-status \
  googleapis-common-protos cloudpickle zstandard py4j ruff==0.14.0

Tests that need an optional package skip without it; for the official suites, CI also installs 'plotly<6.0.0' and graphviz==0.20.3.

docs.title: Build the extension
docs.text:
Build the extension with the Rust requirements above, and copy it into the package. Repeat this after every change to the Rust code, including the Python sources that the extension embeds (crates/pyspark-rs/src/row.py and values.py):

cargo build -p pyspark-rs --release
cp target/release/lib_pyspark.dylib python/pyspark/_pyspark.so   # macOS
cp target/release/lib_pyspark.so python/pyspark/_pyspark.so      # Linux

python/ is then a working pyspark package. CI puts it on PYTHONPATH rather than installing it, which keeps it apart from any other pyspark in the environment:

PYTHONPATH=$(pwd)/python python -c "import pyspark; print(pyspark.__file__)"

To build a wheel instead, run maturin build --release --out dist, which reads [tool.maturin] in pyproject.toml (see Installation).

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
Run the tests from python/. The offline suites, tests/test_*_offline.py and tests/test_arrow_handoff.py, need no server:

cd python
TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest tests/test_*_offline.py tests/test_arrow_handoff.py
TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest tests/test_dropin_offline.py -k pickle   # a subset

The live suites, tests/test_*_e2e.py, run against the local server and skip without SPARK_REMOTE:

SPARK_REMOTE=sc://localhost:15002 TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest tests/test_*_e2e.py

CI runs the test files that its workflows name (coverage.yml for the offline suites, build_python_connect.yml for the live ones), so add a new test to an existing file, or add a new file to the workflow: a guard step of each fails when an offline file (test_*_offline.py or test_arrow_handoff.py) or a live one (test_*_e2e.py) is in no list. CI also measures the coverage of the hand-written shim within the scope of python/.coveragerc, over the offline suites, and fails below the floor that coverage.yml sets:

TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m coverage run --rcfile=.coveragerc -m pytest \
  tests/test_*_offline.py tests/test_arrow_handoff.py
python -m coverage report --rcfile=.coveragerc

docs.title: Run the official PySpark tests
docs.text:
On every pull request, CI runs Apache Spark's own Connect test suites twice: against the drop-in's classes, and with official PySpark sending its requests through the Rust transport. Run the files that cover your change with scripts/run_official_tests.py, from the repository root. --spark is an Apache Spark tree with the tests under python/: CI clones the v4.3.0 tag, and the unpacked distribution has the same test files.

RUST_PYSPARK_SO=$(pwd)/python/pyspark/_pyspark.so TZ=UTC python scripts/run_official_tests.py \
  --dropin --spark "$SPARK_HOME" --remote sc://localhost:15002 \
  --only pyspark/sql/tests/connect/test_parity_column.py

Without --dropin, the file runs through the transport instead. Without --only, the whole suite runs, which takes about an hour on CI (build_python_connect.yml has CI's exact options). The known failures are listed in scripts/dropin_known_failures.txt and scripts/parity_known_failures.txt. Any other failure fails CI, and the runner reports listed tests that now pass, to be removed from the list.

docs.title: Vendored and generated code
docs.text:
Many modules under python/pyspark are verbatim copies of PySpark 4.3.0, such as pyspark.pandas, pyspark.cloudpickle and much of pyspark.ml and pyspark.errors, and so is Spark's spatial reference system registry that the Rust crate embeds, crates/spark-connect/src/srs_registry.csv. Do not edit them: they are listed in scripts/check_vendored_upstream.sh (and the Python ones in the ruff excludes of pyproject.toml), and CI fails when one that the script lists differs from the v4.3.0 tag (the script fetches it from GitHub):

bash scripts/check_vendored_upstream.sh

Fix a behavior in the Rust core (crates/spark-connect), in the bindings (crates/pyspark-rs) or in a hand-written shim instead, and not by monkey-patching a Rust class from Python.

python/pyspark/sql/connect/functions/_generated.py and crates/pyspark-rs/src/dispatch_generated.rs are generated from crates/spark-connect/src/functions.rs. Regenerate them after changing a function there; CI runs the same command with --check:

python scripts/gen_fn_dispatch.py --pyspark-src "$SPARK_HOME/python"

Each optional argument of a PySpark function has a typed form there too: scripts/tests/test_gen_fn_dispatch.py fails on an optional parameter of a function of python/pyspark/sql/connect/functions/builtin.pyi that no Rust function of its name or of its forms takes, unless OPTIONAL_ARGS_OTHERWISE of the generator gives the reason. A form of more trailing Columns goes into OPTIONAL_ARG_VARIANTS, whose arm picks it by the number of arguments, and another form into NOT_DISPATCHED and OPTIONAL_ARG_FORMS.
